items.body: Geology and music often operate in symmetry; we tend to write of “sedimentary layers of sound” and “geological shifts.” In January, we reviewed Paleo Soul, a rock album by Washington geologist Barry Walker Jr. This month, we turn to Scottish musician Intertoto, who references the pioneering work of James Hutton while creating electronic pieces that imitate their corresponding landscapes. The key to both the geography and the music is change, though for obvious reasons the music shifts much swifter than its subjects. “Raw Lunar Concrete” opens the set in sedate fashion, referencing theories about materials that might allow construction on the moon. This immediate sci-fi angle tips the listener into speculative thinking: not just the history of the land, but its possible future. The album takes off with “Condor Launch,” inspired by the RM Condor Marine Base in East Argus, home to numerous squadrons since its opening in 1940. Suddenly, Siccar Point becomes a techno album, but the artist won’t remain there for long. After the appealing club vibe of “Cloud Chamber,” which shifts to the adjacent field of particle physics, the variety of timbres begins to increase, preceded by that track’s gradual recession. “Fold” features LabLab and dives into dub, as if mining the boulders and discovering previously hidden minerals. “Metallic Veins” is calmer, imitating the imperceptible shifts of metamorphosis with tiny rivers of electronic sound. In one sense, the track is the opposite of “Condor Launch;” in another, it uses the same elements, but slowed, thinned, rearranged. This and “Redox Dub” are the most intriguing cuts of the set, despite being the least immediate; to listen is to experience a sense of discovery. The closing “Foraber,” based on Hutton’s eureka moment at Siccar Point, splits the difference between ambient and electronic, lacking only the drums that would make it a club cut. The addition and subtraction of elements throughout the set is its greatest asset, highlighting the impact of slow, incremental change. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Some release an album a month, while others release an EP every couple of years. art test belongs to the latter group. 2024’s fever dreams collected a series of carefully curated singles, and 2026’s foreign lands does the same, acting as a tiny mix tape. The instrumental hip-hop timbre remains in full effect, while the focus is on Middle Eastern rhythms, a purposeful nod to current events. “across the oil fields” is especially timely in its title and bittersweet tone. The world continues to rely on oil, the control continues to shift hands, and art test conveys the melancholic undercurrent of a person who has seen the same scenarios play out again and again, generation after generation. The title track offers its own semantic twist; to Western nations, the Middle East is comprised of “foreign lands,” while the opposite is true when the perspectives are flipped. The track combines Western beats with Eastern strings, offering a third alternative. Older readers may remember a similar time in music, around the turn of the century, when empathy for people around the world was translated into dance music. In the modern era, the very idea of a “ceasefire” seems open to interpretation. Over the past few weeks, many have been called, many have been broken, and some have been broken while the antagonists have insisted that they have not. The entire system of negotiation is flawed. In the track of the same name, optimism is replaced by forlorn resignation, emphasizing the “down” in “downtempo.” By ending in “plumes of smoke,” art test communicates trepidation, but the very existence of the music is a testimony of hope. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Photo: Hilary Scott   Nordic Boomers at Tanglewood Festival of Contemporary Music July 27, 2026 Published in Sequenza 21 By Christian Carey   LENOX – The annual Festival of Contemporary Music concludes with an orchestra concert by the Tanglewood Music Center Orchestra. This year, the festival was curated by Esa-Pekka Salonen, and featured themed programs spotlighting emerging composers, Gen X creators, and Monday’s concert, “Nordic Boomers,” dedicated to fifty and sixty-something Scandinavian composers. Most were colleagues of Salonen from his early days as a student composer. These connections were fruitful, but each composer forged their own path, as was evidenced by the FCM concert. Magnus Lindberg’s Serenades (2020) was curiously named, as it had a muscular demeanor that seemed at odds with its title. Salonen conducted, bringing out details of its vivid orchestration and soaring lines. The piece contained a small quote from Beethoven’s Opus 111. The same source reference point would play a large role in a piece later on in the program. Hans Abrahamsen’s let me tell you (2013), in a libretto crafted by Paul Griffiths, is a setting of the words spoken by the character Ophelia in Shakespeare’s Hamlet. One of Abrahamsen’s best known works, it contains a challenging, wide-ranging and expressively intricate part for solo soprano. Alexandra Henderson sang its demanding and declamatory lines with thoughtful interpretative skill, and displayed plummy low notes and a well-supported upper register. Lauren Smith conducted with nuanced attention to dynamics and phrasing. Anders Hillborg’s Kongsgaard Variations (2006) used the aforementioned quotation, from the arietta movement from Beethoven’s Opus 111 piano sonata, as the basis for a series of variations that he considered meditations rather than the often found developing trajectory of the form. A string orchestra piece, its expert writing was deployed in a variety of playing demeanors. A particularly attractive section featured solo violin, viola, and cello trading folk style melodies in a manner reminiscent of the music played on a Hardinger fiddle, Norway’s national instrument. Elsewhere were neoclassical, minimal, pastoral and modernist variations of the Beethoven theme, some allowing it center stage if slightly morphed, with it instead being submerged in others. Julian Gilewski conducted an effusive, shimmering version of Hillborg’s abundantly attractive piece. The concert concluded with Salonen’s Cello Concerto (2016), conducted by the composer. Written for Yo-Yo Ma, the piece has an extraordinarily challenging solo part. Senja Rummakainen played it with impressive virtuosity and admirable commitment. Cello concertos are notorious for balance issues, but Salonen’s comprehensive knowledge of the orchestra made space both for multihued and powerful orchestral passages and vivid solo writing. The second movement included electronics, with looping of seagull glissandos, an extended technique, interweaving into knots of sound. The third movement features something of a second soloist, with percussionist Patrick Sorah playing bongos, sharing center stage with Rummakainen, his syncopated performance ricocheting in mercurial duets with the cellist. The Festival Orchestra was well-prepared and performed the formidable program with musicality and consummate professionalism. Salonen’s curation of the whole FCM was inspired, and one hopes that he remains a part of Tanglewood’s activities for many years to come. Christian Carey The post Tanglewood Festival of Contemporary Music – Nordic Boomers appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: Saudade is usually a backward-facing feeling, a longing for what has passed. Matu Miranda points it the other way. On “Céu Azulzin” the Brazilian singer and guitarist treats that longing as forward motion, a pull toward somewhere rather than a mourning for something lost. Miranda’s own writing pulls MPB together with jazz, soul and the music of the Northeast. He shares “Céu Azulzin” with Josyara, who comes from Juazeiro in Bahia, the town that raised João Gilberto, and plays with a percussive right hand rooted in the Afro-Brazilian music of the Bahian Recôncavo. Producer Leonardo Marques recorded it at his Ilha do Corvo studio, keeping the sound warm and organic, the two guitars and voices held close together. “Céu Azulzin” is the second single from Apuama, out 4 September, an album built as a travel diary about making a home while staying in motion. The single holds one piece of that journey: the kind of home you carry with you instead of returning to. items.body: Karate Boogaloo have been playing together since they were schoolboys, in the same Melbourne high school maths class, which is the sort of fact most bands turn into a claim about chemistry. Ask what twenty years of it buys them and Henry Jenkins offers elbow grease and luck, and reckons anyone could do what they do. Except only they can… What they do is instrumental funk and soul: bass, drums, organ and guitar, cut to tape, with nobody singing over the top. It runs in both directions. Across three volumes of the KB’s Mixtapes series the four of them play by hand the records hip-hop producers sampled, and away from KB, they cut new library music as Frollen Music Library for producers to sample in turn, which is how their playing reached ScHoolboy Q‘s “Smile” and Leon Thomas’s Mutt. Access All Areas, out on 9 October, holds to that and clears out the rest. Eleven tracks, and as the release notes have it, “if a tune became convoluted, to the bin it went”. It comes through Colemine Records in Loveland, Ohio and College of Knowledge Records in Coburg, Melbourne, the second album the two labels have shared. For the first time the band handed the recording to someone else. Alex Bennett cut it at Sound Recordings in Castlemaine, on tape machines built between the 1950s and the 1980s, all of them kept running by his own hand. Jenkins plays bass, Hudson Whitlock drums, Callum Riley organ, Darvid Thor guitar. They got here the long way, first as the rhythm section of The Cactus Channel, then Hold Your Horses in 2024. With Access All Areas a few months out, we put a handful of questions to the band, and Jenkins answered for all four, correcting half the rules KB are known for, keeping Thor’s fugues off the record, and leaving the question of why Melbourne sounds like this to a local historian who does not yet exist… You’ve been playing together since you were preteens in the same high school maths class, and the new record marks nearly twenty years of that. What can four people who’ve known each other that long do musically that a newer band simply can’t fake? We’re afraid it’s difficult for us to make that claim, with a little bit of elbow grease anyone can do what we do. Luck has been the key ingredient, it has come careening our way on many occasions. It has to if you’re blessed to play music with your best mates for as long as we have. KB started as the rhythm section of The Cactus Channel and got described early on as a “side project”. At what point did it stop feeling like a side thing and become its own animal? We were originally a cover band and a cover band only. The Meters, Booker T & The MG’s, etc. Then one day we wrote a song called “Stay Healthy” and everything changed. We crossed the River Rubicon that day. The band famously imposes strict rules and guidelines on itself: tape only, no plug-ins, no edits, mono releases, four instruments and no vocalist. Where did that manifesto come from, and does the discipline ever feel like a cage rather than a tool? We’re suckers for strict rules but we’ll have to correct a few of those. We record to tape, however we do mix on the computer and we do use plug-ins. No weird plug-ins though, just Waves Doppler. The mixtapes are mono, the albums are stereo, and vocalists are expensive, rightly so. As all good manifestos are, ours is a work in process, and may it forever be. Some rules are carrots, some are sticks, KB needs both. The KB’s Mixtapes series flips hip-hop samples and film and TV themes back into instrumentals. Talk us through how you pick what to reinterpret, and how far you’ll twist something before it stops being recognisable. Imagine the film 12 Angry Men but with four guys arguing about which song to include on an obscure funk mixtape, now picture the exact opposite of that, it’s somewhere in between. When it comes to how far we’ll go, we’ll twist it until it breaks, put it back together, and then hit record. You’ve said the aim with a cover is to bend a well-known tune almost beyond recognition but not quite. Is there one you pushed too far, or one you couldn’t crack no matter how hard you tried? There’s a mountain of tunes we couldn’t crack, we can’t recall them all. We tried making an album called Come With Us, Let’s Terraform Venus and Mars, uncrackable. Access All Areas is out on 9 October through Colemine Records and College of Knowledge Records, and you’ve called it a haiku where Hold Your Horses was an epic. What made you want to strip things down this time, and what got binned in the process? All four of us were on the bus, the 504, and all of the people on the bus started singing “99 Bottles of Beer On The Wall”, we all locked eyes, inhaled, and in unison said: “Access”. Easiest decision we’ve ever made. You’ve said anything convoluted went in the bin and only tunes that could be hummed by anyone survived. What’s an example of something you loved but cut because it failed that test, and did any of you fight to keep it? Darvid composes fugues for fun, and they’re frighteningly beautiful. The world will be subjected to their majesty one day but not on this record. Darvid understands. Access All Areas is the first record you’ve made with an engineer outside the four of you, working with Alex Bennett at Sound Recordings in Castlemaine. What changes when you hand even a small part of the process to someone else? Of all Alex’s incredible traits, and there are many, perhaps the best is that from the first step into his building you feel like you’re at home and in a space you can be yourself in. It’s a wonderful studio and he’s a magnificent engineer. We could sing Alex’s praises all day. Beyond the obvious Booker T & The MG’s and The Meters lineage, there’s a lot of European film music and library music in your DNA. Which of those less-obvious influences do people miss, and who should they be digging into? A favourite at the moment is Jack Arel, a wonderful French composer who we can’t recommend enough. Melbourne’s instrumental soul world is unusually tight, bands sharing members, one studio ecosystem, College of Knowledge Records holding it together. Why do you think that particular sound took root in Melbourne specifically, rather than anywhere else? There are funky roots that go deep in this town, deeper than we know we’re sure. The answer to the question unfortunately evades us right now but something tells us there might be a lovely local historian on this very case! Eyes peeled everyone. For readers outside Australia who maybe only know KB, Surprise Chef and a few other acts, which up-and-coming Melbourne acts should they be paying attention to right now, in or out of your immediate circle? To name only the first that comes to mind, Kasinda Faase is a local legend, everyone must listen to Kasinda’s music or else. How would you describe the state of Melbourne’s music scene right now to someone who’s never been? And where in the city should they actually go to feel it? If Karate Boogaloo ran the world every record store owner and most live music venue proprietors would receive a wheelie bin full of Nobel Peace Prizes. Two bins for the places that do both! They’re the best and they’re the reason Melbourne feels great. If we listen to them we’ll all be swimming in non-stop good times. Forget the funk canon for a second. What have the four of you actually had on repeat this year, and would any of it surprise us? If we could forget it we would, trust us, it’s easier said than done. Just kidding, we don’t want to forget it at all! We love all kinds of music, the weirder the better. Except any music with even a skerrick of “A.I.” in it, that’s the other kind of weird. No thank ye. Twenty years in, with a new album about to land, what does the next 20 years have in store? If we play our cards right and we’re the recipients of even more luck that we don’t deserve, we might just get to do the same thing all over again. Hopefully we’ll all hear a voice from the sky bellow “pull it up!” We always close with a tricky one. In a few words, how would you introduce Karate Boogaloo to someone who’s never heard you before? Karate Boogaloo try to play stock standard instrumental funk music and miss spectacularly every time. Listen along as they work on their aim.   Access All Areas arrives on 9 October via Colemine Records and College of Knowledge Records The album is available to pre-order, alongside the rest of Karate Boogaloo's catalogue, on Bandcamp   The post Interview: Q&A with Karate Boogaloo – “Some Rules Are Carrots, Some Are Sticks” (July 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by James007 — The Watcher I've had a week to listen to this album on EKGPulse and I have to admit I was wrong. When the album was announced, I thought "great, another listenable effort from Eric." I had purchased and enjoyed his previous albums. His work on excellent prog gems like "Lost", "Godspeed", and "Escape" all provided a backdrop of solid craftmanship and technical brilliance with the anticipation of the next chapter along those lines. I was wrong. This was the next level. Perhaps hanging around with Neal and Randy and Mike and Diego helped.... maybe. I'll admit to being an EK "homer" because of his participation in NMB and Temic, but I did not expect THIS. There is true genius in this record. The Overture paints such a wonderful tone to start the album and as each movement takes flight to leave its mark you know you'll be listening to this album again and again. When "The One That Sees It All Alive" hits, the brilliance of this record is finally revealed. The coda of "Fade to Stillness" completes the journey with a sense of peace. The melodies throughout this record are next level greatness. The fact that EK plays everything on this album reminds me of the first time I listened to Jon Anderson's "Olias of Sunhillow" and the awe revealed in one person's inspiration and genius. Yeah, I was wrong. I listen to a bunch of Prog.... in fact, that's about all I listen to. This is a top 3 Prog album for 2026. I'd stack this one up against anything I've heard this year... anything. Yeah, I was wrong. And I pray I'm wrong again and again. Nicely done, sir.

items.body: Review by D0BR0 — Flawless album. The lyrics and the album title make you think like good progressive rock does. Connecting with the powerfully deep, legend of Thor. Deep ideas about creation. As a child creates itself, real magic does occur as it is creating itself. Schizophrenia is also creation and the only way to "get to heaven now". Do not be afraid to add to, create and test your mind. The chosen become young again when they are altered but it is possible to rise from and funnel this lackadaisical play into more direct creative output. It is possible to become the bane of darkness mankind.After someone mentioned A Tab in the Ocean in a top prog list I was on the lookout for them. I was lucky enough to find Magic is a Child, A Tab in the Ocean and Remember the Future all on vinyl. Not too expensive at the time (Past 2005). I had Journey to the center to the Eye on cd. And would later buy Recycler brand new on cd.I remember hearing Magic is a Child in a certain altered state of mind in the morning. With all the things I think about, the lyrics just confirmed it for me and my mind was blown. Instant classic. I hung on every word. The same thing happened with Remember the Future as I aligned with my own narrative of what it meant to me based on my personal life. Easy to add new ideas when you were meant to discover something. The vocals took me awhile to get into but once I did he has a unique, kind of quavering voice. The musicianship is TIGHT on Magic is a Child. These guys are the best of the best.I recently picked up ...Sounds like This and Down to earth on MP3 cheap and it is like coming back home with all these extended jam sessions. Something very special about these guys. Contributed to who I am as I sift through things that may or may not directly speak to me.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Late Night Laments' is a 2020 studio album from Tim Bowness, and it follows up two really solidreleases of his - 'Lost In the Ghost Light' and 'Flowers at the Scene', both of which exhibited abeautifully nostalgic art rock dynamic, within which the haunting enunciated vocals of Bownessbecame one of the defining qualities of the albums. Now, the problem with 'Late Night Laments' isthat the music isn't really developed any further. In fact, this record barely distinguishes itselffrom its predecessors - it is mellow, laid-back, and dreamy, a kind of poppy singer-songwriterexperiment. Bowness is joined by keyboardist Brian Hulse, by the way, who is the primary albumcollaborator.The songs are textured and light, enveloped in a moody atmosphere with subtle ambient undertones.Furthermore, the use of electronic elements is also prevalent, which recalls some of the classic 90sNo-Man releases. I like how Bowness' voice is emphasized by the minimal instrumentation, as it makesfor a moving and effective delivery, but this aspect of the album might be deemed uninspiring bylisteners expecting something more upbeat and eclectic. Of the songs appearing on this LP, Idefinitely enjoyed 'I'm Better Now', 'Darkline', 'Never a Place', and 'Hidden Life' (which aresomewhat darker than the rest of the album). 'Late Night Laments' is a record that demands aparticular mood in order to be appreciated completely, as it leans a little too heavily on thedream-pop influence of its predecessors.

items.body: Review by FrancescoProg — The Aether are an instrumental project from Milan that is making waves with its third studio album, a record that marks a real turning point in their journey begun in 2021. This new work explores a fascinating sonic territory, a refined blend of progressive rock, Northern European jazz-rock, Canterbury sounds, post-rock and ambient electronica.In 2026, with Luminol Records, "III" arrived, the album of maturity, closing a trilogy of instrumental avant-garde. After the post-rock debut of 2023 and the cosmic atmospheres of "Trans-Neptunian Objects" (2024), the quartet ? made up of Andrea Ferrari, Andrea Grumelli, Andrea Serino and Teo Ravelli ? decided to explore a more human and instinctive dimension, setting aside complex concepts.In 2025, the band isolated themselves for long sessions of collective improvisation, minimizing pre-packaged writing. To capture the spontaneous energy typical of jazz bands, they chose to record everything live, with no digital editing or computer fixes. The raw tracks were then refined, mixed and mastered while keeping intact the original punchy dynamics, a blend of the Canterbury sound and Northern European jazz.During the post-production of "Vogon", the band decided to add a touch of originality by involving Claudio Milano, for an avant-garde vocal performance in recitar cantando. Added to this are the flute contributions by Rosarita Crisafi in the opening track "Oort Cloud". These collaborations define the album's experimental and choral nature."III" is an album that plays with expectations, abandoning the classic narrative structure of a concept album to dive into abstraction, into "continuous flow" and into the very essence of the human being, and it invites an inner journey, discovering spontaneity and the "self-generative power" of music.A river of sounds flowing nonstop, with no precise destination. That's exactly the effect created by the music of "III": abstract, fluid, a collective stream born from the 2025 improvisations. The tracks evoke mental landscapes, ranging from cinematic atmospheres to meditative silences and sudden bursts of chaotic, distorted energy. A bit like a film unfolding in our mind, with images following one another in an unpredictable harmony.The album gives great importance to silence and to the resonances between notes, using silence as a blank space on which music can paint, creating a unique and evocative atmosphere.But the real concept of "III" is human interaction, the magic that happens when musicians play together in the same room. No algorithms, no hyper-edited computer music: here live expressiveness is valued, the spontaneous mistake, the musicians' physical togetherness. An authentic, engaging experience that conveys all the energy of the moment.Even though instrumental, the album evokes conceptual suggestions through the titles and the few textual inserts. Take for example "Panta Rei", which translates into music Heraclitus' philosophical idea that "everything flows", constantly changing shape, starting from a jazz opening and flowing into a hypnotic ending. Or "La M�lancolie Du Petit Prince", a tribute to Saint-Exup�ry's work, trying to capture the poetic loneliness and innocence of the Little Prince. And then there's "Vogon", a track inspired by the alien race from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, with Claudio Milano's avant-garde voice reciting a cryptic text, the only explicit literary element in a sea of instrumental sounds."III" is a record that tastefully blends modern progressive rock, European jazz and instrumental post-rock. It's almost entirely instrumental, acoustic and analog, and it stands out for a crazy dynamism, with moments of deep silence alternating with scream-worthy sonic explosions.The influence of Northern European jazz is felt right away in the handling of space and silence. The open chords of the Fender Rhodes and the laid-back bass lines create ethereal, suspended atmospheres.The band takes up the rhythmic complexity and odd meters typical of classic progressive rock (Soft Machine and King Crimson), but without sounding nostalgic or like a copy.Many tracks develop with long crescendos typical of modern post-rock, where layers of distorted guitars and minimal electronics build up until they culminate in imposing, hypnotic finales that leave you speechless.The analog warmth of the Fender Rhodes electric piano and the fretless bass creates a soft, jazzy harmonic bed that wraps around you.The Chapman Stick makes it possible to combine complex bass lines and geometric textures, adding a unique touch to the sound.The guitar ranges from clean, cinematic arpeggios to powerful distortions that give you goosebumps. The drums don't just keep time, but constantly interact with the other instruments, integrating subtle electronic nuances that enrich the whole.The album mainly moves between Jazz-Rock and contemporary Progressive Rock. Being an experimental work in constant evolution, it sits at the crossroads of three major musical genres:Avant-Prog / Progressive Rock, for the complexity of its structures, the use of odd meters and the long instrumental suites that recall the historic Canterbury Scene.Modern Jazz (ECM School), for the strong improvisational component, the use of open, warm chords and a handling of silence typical of Northern European jazz.Instrumental and Cinematic Post-Rock, for the development of the tracks through atmospheric dynamics and long "crescendos" that culminate in imposing walls of distorted guitars and minimal electronics.A modern formula that combines the refined technique of jazz with the visceral power of alternative rock.In my opinion, three tracks from "III" stand out as the most representative of the album:Cinq Teintes, Quatre Cadres, with the excellent interplay between electric guitar and Fender Rhodes, managing to create exotic, hypnotic atmospheres without overdoing the virtuosity.La M�lancolie Du Petit Prince, the calmest and most ambient track, with the skillful use of atmospheric electronics and a cultured, pianistic approach.Vogon, the most disorienting and original piece. Even if it breaks with the record's completely instrumental nature thanks to Claudio Milano's avant-garde recitar cantando, it shows experimental courage and a strong theatrical charge."III" is an album that invites active listening, letting yourself be carried by the flow of the music and discovering the endless possibilities hidden between the notes. A unique, unforgettable experience that will leave you wanting to listen again and again. Excellent album!

items.body: Bruckner began his Symphony No. 7 in September 1881, soon after finishing the Sixth, and completed the finale in the late summer of 1883. He was fifty-nine, and his symphonies were still meeting resistance in Vienna. This is the work that changed his fortunes, and it did so not at home but in Germany. Arthur Nikisch conducted the premiere in Leipzig in December 1884. The success was genuine, though not unanimous. Hermann Levi’s Munich performance ten weeks later settled the matter. The score asks for pairs of woodwinds, four horns, trumpets and trombones, a contrabass tuba, timpani and strings. The weight comes from the depth of the brass rather than sheer numbers. Four Wagner tubas supply the work’s unique color, utilized here for the first time in a symphony and featured only in the Adagio and the finale. The first movement opens with one of the longest melodies in the repertoire, an arch given to the horn and cellos over a hushed string tremolo. The finale closes by bringing that same theme back in its original solemn form. The Adagio was begun in the expectation of Wagner’s death and finished after the news came, and Bruckner described its closing pages as music of mourning for the master. The Adagio’s great climax carries a cymbal clash, a triangle and a timpani roll that were not in his first draft. They came from his conductor-disciples and were entered later on a slip pasted into the score in his own hand. Robert Haas struck them out in his 1944 edition, and Leopold Nowak restored them ten years later. Conductors have taken sides ever since, which is why the peak of the slow movement lands differently from one recording to the next. Here are The Classic Review editorial team’s recommendations for the best recordings of Bruckner’s Symphony No. 7. Staatskapelle Dresden, Eugen Jochum Jochum’s Dresden Seventh is rightfully remembered for its extraordinary Adagio. The central movement glows from within, its long crescendo unfolding on brass tones that are simultaneously burnished and unmistakably human. What elevates this reading beyond a mere exercise in atmospheric beauty is the relentless architectural tension Jochum sustains across the entire canvas. The glorious Adagio never feels isolated, instead arriving as an inevitable emotional destination. He achieves this by subtly flexing the tempo to delineate each structural shift, an interpretive choice that has fascinated listeners for decades. This remains a definitive benchmark against which other interpretations are constantly judged. Jochum Amazon Presto Apple Berlin Philharmonic, Günter Wand Wand brought decades of hard-won Bruckner experience to his guest appearances in Berlin. That deep familiarity shines through in the sheer breadth of his phrasing. He allows every musical span to breathe fully without ever letting the underlying pulse sag. The orchestra retains an astonishing transparency even during the heaviest sections, ensuring quiet woodwind figures in the Scherzo hold their distinct place rather than vanishing. Opting for the edition that leaves the Adagio’s climax entirely to strings and brass, he builds the peak so convincingly that listeners miss no extra percussion. Only in the final bars does the texture slightly tilt as the trumpets surge forward. Wand Amazon Presto Apple Vienna Philharmonic, Herbert von Karajan Karajan recorded the Seventh three times in the studio. This Vienna account, taped in 1989, stands apart as a personal farewell. Where his earlier Berlin versions felt monumental and grand, this interpretation glows with a fragile grace. The Adagio expands into a sublime elegy that retains its pristine architectural form throughout. Bathed in the warm sheen of the Vienna strings, the sound offers remarkable clarity and depth. Some listeners find the finale slightly less cohesive than the preceding movements. Yet few recordings manage to hold raw symphonic power and delicate vulnerability in such exquisite equilibrium. Karajan Amazon Presto Apple Berlin Radio Symphony Orchestra, Riccardo Chailly Chailly favors broad tempos, yet he never allows the phrasing to go slack. A deep, steady momentum carries the first movement forward, giving even its most sprawling sections a clear sense of destination. This structural clarity is precisely what makes the recording so admired, alongside audio engineering that remains stunningly realistic. The dividing factor is the emotional temperature. Some find this studio account slightly reserved compared to the thrilling spontaneity Chailly often brings to the concert hall. Regardless of where you stand on that restraint, his grasp of the symphony’s architecture is never in question. Chailly Amazon Presto Apple Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Bernard Haitink Haitink’s second Amsterdam recording stands as a quiet masterpiece of the catalog. The Concertgebouw delivers an even, luminous warmth from the opening bar to the final chord. Haitink navigates Bruckner’s great sonic blocks so seamlessly that the symphony flows without ever feeling segmented. The Adagio alone justifies adding this album to any collection. Its towering climax, cymbals included, is balanced with rare taste and proportion. If you prize sheer lyrical beauty over thunderous theatricality, begin your journey here. Haitink Amazon Presto Apple Vienna Philharmonic, Nikolaus Harnoncourt Striking velocity defines Harnoncourt’s interpretive approach from the very first notes. He moves noticeably faster than most peers while shining a revealing spotlight on the orchestra’s inner voices. Consequently, the opening theme carries an unsettling edge rather than standard serene devotion. Clean audio engineering preserves a natural perspective, ensuring the strings never overwhelm subordinate details. The cymbal crash at the peak of the Adagio is omitted, but listeners receive wonderfully dark Wagner tubas and a fierce, driving Scherzo. The nimble finale sparkles, powered by triumphant brass playing. Harnoncourt Amazon Presto Apple Munich Philharmonic, Sergiu Celibidache Celibidache’s idiosyncratic style regularly polarizes critical opinion, but this live 1984 concert makes a compelling case for his unique artistic vision. Spanning roughly seventy-four minutes, the performance moves at a famously expansive pace yet miraculously maintains forward momentum. The conductor unfailingly understands the ultimate trajectory of every phrase, shaping lines with complete authority. Munich’s elite instrumentalists respond with flawless execution and immaculate orchestral balance. While this smooth sculpting may occasionally push legato phrasing further than purists prefer, the archival sound is remarkably clear. Even admirers of the slower remake he made a decade later often return to this leaner, earlier one. Celibidache Amazon Presto Apple Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra, Manfred Honeck Few modern releases match this performance for sheer sonic spectacle. Taped in 2022, the recording boasts an enormous dynamic range, keeping complex counterpoint wonderfully clear even during cataclysmic peaks. Honeck builds his climaxes with immense patience and care. In the Adagio, he highlights a recurring phrase echoing the Te Deum, investing each return with distinct character. A rustic, swinging lilt in the Scherzo successfully summons the country dance hidden beneath the score. Minor caveats include an opening movement that feels sluggish at first and a heavily stretched final chord that crosses into engineering excess. Still, it is a formidable state-of-the-art showcase. Read the original review of this album here Honeck Amazon Presto Apple SWR Stuttgart Radio Symphony Orchestra, Kurt Sanderling Although lesser-known than major catalog staples, this Stuttgart release is among the most rewarding. Sanderling strikes the ideal tempo right away and holds it steady throughout. The grave, unhurried Adagio allows the Wagner tubas to deliver a lament of heartbreaking emotional weight. The brilliantly handled finale sets this performance apart from rivals. Sanderling draws sharp contrasts between quick and slow episodes, capturing the movement’s perpetual shift between humor and solemnity. Orchestral balances are so finely judged that no single section swamps another, keeping the vital horn counterlines fully audible. The stunning coda transitions effortlessly from desolation to consolation. Sanderling Amazon Presto Apple Royal Scottish National Orchestra, Georg Tintner Without proper momentum, Bruckner’s Seventh can easily disintegrate into two ponderous slow movements bracketed by faster ones. Tintner masterfully evades this trap by identifying the exact, natural tempo for every musical thought. The opening movement generates substantial power, ensuring the Adagio feels like a logical consequence rather than an abrupt shift in focus. Employing the score edition that strips away added percussion from the slow movement’s climax offers a clear window into an old musicological debate. Both outer movements land their final codas with unerring precision. This thoughtful reading remains exceptionally difficult to fault, offering endless rewards. items.body: Swedish dark synthpop trio Priest will release the single “Python” on August 21 via Blue Nine, the first taste of their fifth studio album, “Altered State Police,” due October 23 on the same label. The announcement follows the band’s US tour supporting Stabbing Westward. “Python” turns surveillance and data collection into subject matter, built around relentless electronics, industrial textures and flashes of ’90s big beat. The track includes a spoken sequence cataloguing a listener’s data: “Terms accepted. Surveillance initiated. Facial data: stored. Iris response: logged. Voice patterns: catalogued. You are now a consumer profile. Thank you for agreeing.” Priest describe it as one of their most direct and danceable songs to date, addressing “what happens when we’ve accepted being watched without even noticing.” “Altered State Police” is designed as a continuous listening experience rather than a loose collection of songs, built around surveillance, political distrust, technological dependence and the boundary between human and machine, with songs written to answer questions raised elsewhere on the record. Neither the single nor the album has surfaced yet on Bandcamp, YouTube or Spotify; Priest’s official site, priestnexus.com, currently carries the “Python” and “Altered State Police” announcement and upcoming tour information. The single follows Priest’s run on the Wither ReWired Tour, the 2026 US trek on which Stabbing Westward re-recorded “Wither Blister Burn + Peel” for its 30th anniversary, with Priest and Acumen Nation as support. Priest ‘Python’: release details “Python” arrives August 21 via Blue Nine as the first single from “Altered State Police,” out October 23 on the same label. No tracklist, credits or formats for the album have been confirmed at the time of writing. About Priest Priest is a dark synthpop trio from Stockholm, Sweden, formed in 2017 by former members of Ghost: vocalist Mercury (previously the bassist known as Water in Ghost) and keyboardist Salt (previously the keyboardist known as Air in Ghost), later joined by keyboardist and programmer Sulfur. The band’s sound draws on 1980s sci-fi synth textures, gothic soundscapes and industrial and cyberpunk elements, distinct from Ghost’s horror-rock theatrics. Priest released its debut album, “New Flesh,” in 2017, followed by the “Obey” EP in 2019 and the album “Cyberhead” in 2020. The band signed to Cleopatra Records in 2021 and released the single “A Signal in the Noise” that December. Further releases include the “Chaos EP,” the live album “Live in Hollywood,” the studio album “Dark Pulse” and, in March 2026, “Body Machine.” Priest has since moved to the label Blue Nine, which issues “Python” and the forthcoming “Altered State Police.” Priest has toured internationally in support of its releases, most recently opening for Stabbing Westward’s Wither ReWired Tour across the United States in 2026. “Python,” out August 21, and “Altered State Police,” out October 23, mark the band’s next chapter under Blue Nine.

items.body: Mexico City-based act My Black Heart Machine has released a new album, Luminance, on Bandcamp. The band describes its own sound as “dark alternative.” The nine-track record went up on 14 July 2026, led by the single “We Should.” Luminance by My Black Heart Machine “Luminance” comprises nine tracks: “Bittersweet,” “Your Last Breath,” “Everytime,” “We Should,” “The Last Thing I’ll See,” “All Hail You,” “Your Shattered Mind,” “Luminance,” and “A Warm Light.” The album is available as a digital release through Bandcamp. My Black Heart Machine pairs ‘Luminance’ with a ‘We Should’ video The album’s first single, “We Should,” comes with an official music video posted to My Black Heart Machine’s own YouTube channel. About My Black Heart Machine My Black Heart Machine is the project of Camilo Montenegro, a composer, producer, and mixing engineer based in Mexico City, Mexico. Montenegro writes, arranges, and performs the material under the My Black Heart Machine name. The project’s prior album, “Anonymous Confessions,” came out on 2 January 2024 and ran ten tracks. “Luminance” is My Black Heart Machine’s newest full-length, released independently through Bandcamp.

items.body: Project Pitchfork, the German dark electro group fronted by Peter Spilles, gets a Project Pitchfork anthology vinyl release: two of its career-spanning compilations pressed to vinyl for the first time. Trisol releases “First Anthology” and “Second Anthology” as limited 3LP sets on 16 October 2026, each capped at 1,000 numbered copies. “First Anthology” was originally issued as a double CD in 2011, drawing on the band’s early years, its own label Candyland Entertainment and its later run on the major-label imprint EastWest. The new vinyl edition spreads 31 tracks across three 180g 12″ black vinyl records, a German audiophile pressing, and includes anthem tracks such as “Timekiller”, “Alpha Omega” and “I Live Your Dream”. The set comes in a gatefold sleeve with printed inner sleeves, and the artwork draws on photos from Peter Spilles’ private archive. “Second Anthology” followed in 2016 as a companion double CD covering the band’s catalogue from 2002 onward, built around the previously unreleased song “What Have We Done” and a remix, “Beholder (Puppet Master Mix)”. Its vinyl counterpart carries 30 tracks over three 180g 12″ records with the same gatefold, printed-inner-sleeve and archive-photo artwork treatment as its companion, and highlights key tracks “Rain”, “Acid Ocean” and “Beholder”. Both anthologies are limited to 1,000 numbered copies and are due through Trisol. Project Pitchfork anthology vinyl arrives ahead of anniversary tour The two anthology vinyls land in the same year Project Pitchfork mark their 35th anniversary. Side-Line previously reported on the band’s Dhyani 35th anniversary reissue, the 2LP deluxe edition of Entities, and the 35 Years in the Heart of Darkness anniversary tour running across Germany from October to December 2026 – the same window in which both anthology vinyls arrive. About Project Pitchfork Project Pitchfork was formed in Hamburg, Germany, by Peter Spilles and Dirk Scheuber, who met in late 1988 and began working together as Project Pitchfork the following year, picking the band’s name at random from a dictionary. The band played its first live show in Hamburg in February 1990 and released the demo “K.N.K.A.” that August. Debut album “Dhyani” followed in May 1991 on Hypnobeat, with second album “Lam-‘Bras” arriving in February 1992 and introducing Patricia Nigiani as a backing vocalist. Third album “Entities” followed six months later. A move to the Off Beat label produced 1994’s “Io,” which gave the band its first German chart entry via the singles “Renascence” and “Carrion,” followed by a lengthy tour. In 1995 Project Pitchfork founded their own label, Candyland Entertainment, releasing “Alpha Omega” the same year and touring in support of Rammstein. “¡Chakra:Red!” (1997) was the first album written as a full group effort and introduced Jürgen Jansen as a permanent member. The band then signed to major-label imprint EastWest for the concept album “Eon:Eon” (1998), whose singles “Steelrose,” “Carnival” and “I Live Your Dream” brought the band German music-TV airplay and an Echo Award nomination for the “Steelrose” video. Project Pitchfork released “Daimonion” (2001) and the “NUN” trilogy centered on “Inferno” (2002), then “Kaskade” (2005) and “Dream, Tiresias!” (2009). By 2011, having wound down Candyland, the band had moved to Trisol, releasing “Continuum Ride” (2010) and “Quantum Mechanics” (2011) – the same year Trisol issued the original “First Anthology” compilation. “Black” (2013) and “Blood” (2014) followed, and in 2016 Trisol released “Second Anthology,” built around the unreleased track “What Have We Done,” alongside 25th-anniversary album “Look Up, I’m Down There.” “Akkretion” (2018) and “Fragment” (2018) opened a further trilogy that closed with 2024’s “Elysium.” Co-founder Dirk Scheuber left the band in March 2021; the current lineup centers on Peter Spilles with Jürgen Jansen, alongside live drummers Achim Färber and Christian “Leo” Leonhardt. Trisol now brings both career-spanning anthologies to vinyl for the first time, due 16 October 2026 as limited, numbered 3LP editions.

items.body: “The doldrums” sounds like a dark room with no windows and no lights. You step inside, lock the door behind you, and extinguish the final seam of light beneath it. At first, the darkness appears empty; then the mind begins furnishing it with everything you hoped to leave outside. Fear searches for something concealed nearby while dread waits for it to reveal itself. Angst returns to the same unanswered question, passion strains against confinement, love becomes fixation, and anguish grows louder because there is nowhere for any of it to go. Beyond that imagined room, the word describes a spell of listlessness or despondency, a period of stagnation, and an equatorial region of calms, squalls, and shifting winds. In its nautical sense, opposing trade winds converge near the equator, leaving sailing ships trapped on windless water. The sails collapse, the hull ceases to advance, provisions diminish, and the crew can see the horizon without drawing any closer to it. The ship and the dark room share one cruelty: an exit can be imagined while remaining unreachable. Goth and post-punk have made lasting music from precisely these states. Fear tightens the bass into a narrow repeating figure; dread occupies the interval before the next drum hit; angst gives the lyric a question it cannot answer; passion swells through distortion; love supplies the reason to remain; anguish comes from recognizing the pattern while continuing to obey it. Black Doldrums is therefore an unusually exact name: music for the locked room and a ship adrift at sea, where the mind returns to familiar pain because familiarity can resemble shelter. Appropriately, London trio Black Doldrums’ latest release, Repetition, centers on the inability to break a pattern. The song is the lead single and opening track of the band’s third studio album, Repetition Compulsion, due November 13th, 2026, via Fuzz Club. The record completes Black Doldrums’ interconnected “State of Mind Trilogy,” following their 2022 debut, Dead Awake, and 2024’s In Limerence. The three albums consider the psychological forces that shape identity, memory, and human connection, with the creative and personal partnership between founding members Kevin Gibbard and Sophie Landers providing their emotional center. As Gibbard explains: “The songs are either about Sophie, for Sophie, or inspired by her.” “Repetition begins with a funereal synthesizer exhalation, a dusky bass tone, and a beat that lands with the bodily insistence of a heart awaiting bad news. A cold guitar figure enters in clipped phrases while bell-like electronics toll far back in the mix. Gibbard’s vocal melody brushes against the severe romanticism of The Sisters of Mercy’s “Marian,” while his softened, reverb-heavy timbre evokes Neil Halstead from Slowdive if he were dragged into a goth club. With each cycle, more haze collects around the vocal until the recording seems to lose its walls. Landers becomes increasingly audible behind Gibbard, turning confession into divided speech. The bass later steps forward with the high-register gravity of Peter Hook on Joy Division’s Closer, particularly the downward pull of “Twenty Four Hours.” Its dense, overdriven attack also evokes Simon Gallup during the Cure’s Pornography-era tour, when his bass occupied the front of the mix as a blunt rhythmic force and a source of dread. Gibbard explains the song’s origin: “The song came from an idea to challenge ourselves to write something around one riff and something dirge-like. It also fit the theme of the album and the topic of repetition by literally experimenting with repetition in the musical sense. The opening line – “is your mind split in two” – is something taken from our conversations on our many long walks around London where Sophie was talking about the psychological term splitting. It seemed to fit the feel of the song and theme of the album so much so it now opens up both the album and our live shows. I consider it very much Sophie’s song because she was the source of inspiration and that’s why we have her backing vocals fairly prominent to create a dual vocal effect. I also had the after-thought to have Sophie mime the first line in the video which is actually her line anyway.” The phrase “is your mind split in two” brings the album’s psychological framework down to one troubling image: a mind unable to reconcile its opposing halves. Landers’s backing vocal gives that division a second body, allowing the song to behave like a thought hearing itself repeated from elsewhere. Its central riff follows the same principle, returning with enough force that familiarity becomes confinement. Filmed by Landers and Gibbard, with the final cut crafted by Landers, the scene begins with Landers gazing directly into the camera, silently delivering the line that sparked the song. Her high-collared white blouse, black straps, braided hair, dramatic eye makeup, and black lipstick create a striking contrast against a nearly empty black background. Gibbard appears dressed in black, with close-cropped blond hair, his face illuminated by pale blue and green lighting. Their portraits alternate between clean digital images and footage rephotographed from a monitor. Vertical scan lines stripe Landers’s face; clipped highlights bleach her features into white and violet; soft focus, projection, and offset copies divide her image across the screen. Gibbard receives similar treatment as his head drifts in and out of the surrounding black. Close-ups of fingers working a bass guitar and a solitary illuminated snare interrupt the faces, then return according to the song’s circular logic. The clip’s most pointed image is a small porcelain pig figurine dropping into the frame and shattering against a black floor. Landers later restores it through editing, only for the descent, impact, and dispersal of its fragments to happen again. The sequence becomes a compact illustration of repetition compulsion: an object returns intact so that the original damage can be recreated. Faces, gestures, instruments, and breakage recur with slight mutations, making repetition the video’s visual grammar as well as the song’s foundation. Watch the video for Repetition below: Repetition Compulsion takes its title from the Freudian concept describing “the unconscious tendency to recreate familiar emotional patterns, destructive behaviours and inherited cycles from the past.” Across eleven songs, Black Doldrums examine the ways these patterns enter relationships, memory, political life, and mental health. “The album invites listeners to confront the echoes of the past while questioning whether those patterns can ever truly be broken,” says Gibbard. The trio draws upon ’80s gothic post-punk, synth-pop, and darkwave, alongside the film music of John Carpenter and Vangelis. Analogue synthesizers, chorus-treated guitars, and driving rhythms give the record a cinematic scale while preserving the melodic directness established across the previous two albums. Repetition Compulsion arrives November 13th, 2026, on 180-gram neon-yellow vinyl limited to 350 hand-numbered copies, 180-gram ultra-clear vinyl, and CD. Pre-order the album here. Repetition Compulsion by Black Doldrums Kevin Gibbard and Sophie Landers formed Black Doldrums in London as a two-piece, combining Gibbard’s guitar and vocals with Landers’s drums and vocals. Their early work drew heavily from dark psychedelia, drone, reverb, and the physical economy of playing as a duo. The addition of bass expanded Black Doldrums into a trio around the recording of Dead Awake, giving the songs a more pronounced post-punk structure. Released through Fuzz Club in 2022, Dead Awake established their colder and more direct studio approach. Its 2024 successor, In Limerence, examined romantic fixation, loss, and the unstable interior life of a relationship. The band subsequently toured extensively across the UK and Europe, including arena dates supporting Archive and their own headlining runs. Repetition Compulsion brings the trilogy to its conclusion while extending those personal questions into inherited behaviour, politics, memory, and mental wellbeing. items.body: When we first heard Analog Dance’s recent single Fall Apart, the song seemed built from passion and pressure: a rigid beat marking the perimeter, bright synthesizers narrowing the available space, and Jonny Castle’s baritone holding its composure while the dancefloor threatens to bend and buckle from its seductive groove. Within Analog Dance’s second album, Mind The Fall, that steamy pressure becomes one element in a larger design. Across eleven tracks and just under forty-five minutes, the London darkwave project turns collapse, concealment, desire, and performance into sensual dark electronic pop, with guitar supplying warmth or frost at carefully chosen moments. Mind The Fall, released July 22 through Poland’s Bat-Cave Productions, follows the project’s 2024 debut, Stranger Minds. Written and recorded in isolation in a wooden cabin in Argentina, the album carries the concentration that distance can bring. Its songs feel secluded and interior, while broad drum machines, elastic bass sequences, and clean guitar lines give them considerable physical force. The production is fuller and more exact than before, though the closeness of a private recording remains central to its appeal. In a 2024 interview, Jonny described Analog Dance as an alter ego created to express emotions that words alone could not carry. He also traced the project’s name to the tactile appeal of analog equipment and the ability of synthesizers to stir feeling and movement. Mind The Fall gives that idea its clearest form yet: the machines set bodies in motion, while his voice reveals the cost of maintaining control. The titles supply their own vocabulary. Wires and screens suggest mediation; masks and shows invoke presentation; decay, rot, and falling apart name what lies beneath. Even “A Clean Version of Hell” turns damage into something polished enough for display. These phrases create a thread across the record, and the music follows suit, pairing immaculate surfaces with uneasy motion underneath. “Ghost on a Wire” opens with low, fluttering synthesizers that carry a faintly occult charge, followed by a broad drum-machine strike and a simple rising-and-falling guitar figure. Jonny’s baritone enters deep, lush, and close, drawing the ear toward the center of the mix. The melody is economical enough to lodge after one pass, while the production gives every layer room to register. As an opener, it introduces the album’s governing attraction: machine precision warmed by a voice carrying unmistakable appetite. “A Clean Version of Hell” begins in metal and glass, patiently arranging hard-edged effects and cool high-register tones before a heavy ’80s drum pattern and rounded melodic bass take command. Crystalline guitar phrases hang above the rhythm as Jonny brings deep new-wave romance to the center. The title’s contradiction—hell sanitized, pain made presentable—anticipates the record’s later concern with screens, masks, and performance, while the music could easily accompany the most intimate scene in an unmade late-night thriller. “Fall Apart” gains additional meaning from its place in the sequence. The severe elegance remains: a rigid beat draws the room, the synthesizers constrict it, and unease passes from bass to percussion to the open space around the vocal. Its supple club gait occasionally recalls Boy Harsher’s more sensual turns, though Jonny’s elongated phrasing and the clean post-punk guitar keep the song firmly within Analog Dance’s own language. Positioned between “A Clean Version of Hell” and “Behind the Screen,” the lead single becomes the album’s hinge, connecting polished catastrophe to private longing. “Behind the Screen” fades in gradually, assembling drums, bell-like chimes, and broad, glassy pads in measured layers. The mood brings to mind a romantic scene from 2011’s Drive, with city light sliding across a windshield as a high guitar line curls upward through smoke. Jonny holds his notes longer here, allowing earnest tenderness to replace some of the album’s usual reserve. The result produces a quiet rush of serotonin, spacious and enveloping, with each element entering at precisely the right moment. “Five-Star Mask” starts with rippling synthesizers that recall S U R V I V E scoring one of Stranger Things’ dreamier passages. A single DX7-like digital preset flashes past—before the full dance beat settles in. Drums and bass carry the weight as a supple synthwave melody continues below Jonny’s low, sultry vocal. Glinting guitar and a buoyant ascending-and-descending motif complete an intimate midtempo dance, made for two people moving together while the surrounding room recedes. “Intimate Decay” lowers the temperature with wavering upper-register tones and a deep electronic hum, then suspends the arrangement for a breath before a rubbery bass sequence begins. Cold jolts repeat, the drums shudder, and a brief baroque figure rises and falls before Analog Dance’s favored high-register guitar enters. Jonny sustains his phrases above the accumulating layers until the texture feels nearly physical. The title’s pairing of closeness and decomposition could stand as the album’s thesis, and the track renders that friction with particular tenderness. “Same War Within” opens on gauzy pads, pinpoint synth notes, and a heavy kick before claps and a rippling bass line steer it toward Italo disco. Guitar serves as an accent at first, leaving generous space around the low vocal. A little over a minute in, the arrangement changes its balance: a burbling figure settles below the mix, the voice drops out, and the guitar takes melodic command before the two rejoin over a cool pad. That sequence of handoffs is among the album’s smartest structural moves, creating development through control rather than grandstanding. “Scenic Crime” eases the pace with subdued synthesizers, a measured drum pattern, and a bass backbone that keeps the song moving. A modest, immediately hummable keyboard melody appears, and the guitar soon traces its outline. The feeling is wistful, suspended somewhere between pleasure and loss, as Jonny’s smooth delivery settles over low melodic undertones and small electronic flourishes drift through the margins. Its emotional ambiguity gives the track its pull; the view is lovely, though something unresolved remains just beyond the frame. “Beautiful Rot” opens with distorted, icy electronics, then answers them with a rapid drum barrage and a muscular dance bass line, making this one of the record’s fastest selections. A buoyant sequence and clear bell tones prepare the entrance of Jonny’s baritone and a clean, chiming guitar, while his quicker vocal phrasing swoops around the percussion. The song turns the album’s central contradiction into movement, placing elegance and deterioration in the same body. Its speed and melodic abundance make it a late-record peak. “The Plastic Show” rides a cycling electronic sequence that remains in place while resonant chimes, low-register strings, and a cleaner guitar line accumulate around it. Jonny initially sounds more detached than he did on “Beautiful Rot,” but his delivery gathers pressure as the song proceeds. Frustration remains contained within the measured arrangement, creating the sense of somebody trying to keep up appearances while emotion presses against the surface. As the record’s clearest invocation of artificial display, it brings the album’s concern with performance into plain view. “Selling the Show” closes the album by fading into broad pads and skittering drums, immediately establishing a cinematic new-wave atmosphere. Metallic bass enters with a melodic bounce, the pace gathers, and Jonny’s voice guides the song through several cleanly placed breaks. Familiar burbling synthesizers and a luminous guitar line return, but the final vocal passages are compressed into a distant, radio-like signal. That treatment leaves the confession mediated and receding, as though private feeling has finally been packaged for transmission. Taken together, Mind The Fall draws openly from the memory of ’80s post-punk, darkwave, synthpop, synthwave, and film music, using those reference points as a working vocabulary. Analog Dance’s identity remains distinct: a low voice with considerable tenderness, forceful electronic drums, lucid guitar, and synthesizers that can suggest glass, smoke, metal, or silk. The album is sensual, emotionally exposed, and highly danceable, with pacing that gives desire and anxiety equal weight. Where Stranger Minds established the dimensions of Jonny’s private world, Mind The Fall brings its architecture into sharper focus. Recurring textures connect the songs, the titles deepen one another, and “Fall Apart” now reads as the center of an album preoccupied with the effort required to remain intact. It is Analog Dance’s most cohesive release so far, a record whose immaculate finish cannot conceal the strain moving underneath. Mind The Fall was released July 22 through Bat-Cave Productions and is available now on all streaming platforms. The physical CD edition can be ordered directly from the label, while the label’s Bandcamp offers a digital edition. Analog Dance credits Crimeframe for recording, production, mixing, and mastering, Rusty Pilgrim for artwork, and Synth Wizrd for design. Listen to Mind the Fall below or via Spotify and order it here. items.body: Diego Romo’s Are The Lovers moves with the heavy, deliberate gait of something crawling out from beneath a nightclub after closing time, wearing somebody else’s leather jacket and carrying a grin that suggests the evening went either very well…or catastrophically wrong. The 24-year-old Chilean artist drags alternative rock, post-punk, synthwave, and gothic excess into the same dim room, then lets them eye one another suspiciously over the bassline. The opening seconds establish a pace somewhere between a stalk and a crawl, allowing each low note to land with the authority of a hostile bouncer. The sinister bass is the song’s center of gravity: thick, slow, and almost indecently physical. Around it, guitars grind without turning the track into a blunt-force exercise, while electronic textures give the production a futuristic chill. Strange sucking sounds appear between phrases, an inspired bit of studio mischief that makes the song feel as though it might latch on to your neck while you are busy admiring the chorus. Romo’s voice hangs above the arrangement in sheets of echo, cool enough to seem composed yet close enough to carry an unmistakable sense of appetite. “This song is what I imagine would happen if Queens of the Stone Age and Nine Inch Nails decided to write a song for sex in the year 2079,” he says. One suspects the year 2079 will involve worse rent, smaller apartments, and considerably less flattering latex wear. Are The Lovers shares Queens of the Stone Age’s narcotic strut and Nine Inch Nails’ industrial unease, but Romo also reaches toward Depeche Mode’s decadent electronics, Type O Negative’s funereal sensuality, and the sleek night-drive menace associated with the late Kavinsky. The Horrors hover nearby in the track’s smeared textures, while the Arctic Monkeys comparison surfaces through its slow, knowing posture. Seduction becomes more interesting when a little spice enters the room. Are The Lovers plods forward with purpose, leaving enough space for every drum hit, vocal echo, and unidentifiable mouth-like noise to register. Listen to Are The Lovers below: Are The Lovers presents Diego Romo as an artist with a firm grasp of atmosphere and a healthy suspicion of daylight. His mix of rock mythology, cyberpunk imagery, vampiric desire, and electronic menace could easily collapse into costume drama, yet the song maintains a sharp sense of control. It is sensual, strange, and slightly ridiculous in precisely the right proportions, which is often where rock music starts behaving properly again. items.body: ZEU’s Existor is an album that begins with the sort of grand private wager rock records used to make before everybody became a brand manager with a ring light: one person, one room, a stack of machines, and enough nerve to build a small city out of doubt. ZEU, pronounced “zoo,” is Matthew Zedolik of Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, and he handles the writing, playing, recording, and production himself. That arrangement can produce either magnificent obsession or twelve tracks of a man arguing with his presets. Here, obsession wins by several lengths. Zedolik describes his approach as “’80s-era Springsteen meets Billy Idol, Depeche Mode, and Sisters of Mercy.” It sounds like a barroom dare issued after somebody fed the jukebox three dollars and locked all the exits. Existor carries that collision with uncommon coherence. Drum machines march beside broad synthesizers, guitars supply muscle and abrasion, and the songs keep returning to direct pop shapes even when the lyrics are busy examining memory, age, desire, disappointment, and the cash-register logic infecting ordinary relationships. Zedolik’s background helps explain the album’s reach. Teenage metal bands taught him weight; The Ordinals gave him bass discipline; American Buffalo Ghost supplied guitar mileage; recording studies in New York sharpened his control over space and arrangement. He brings all of it into these twelve songs without turning the record into a résumé with drums. The parts serve the writing, and the writing keeps moving. Here, contemporary life has turned emotion into an exchange rate, and Existor keeps poking at the price tag until the adhesive comes off. Nobody needs another lecturer with a synthesizer; ZEU prefers hooks sturdy enough to smuggle the argument through the front door. Nostalgia, written in March 2024, marks the beginning of the album’s documented history and establishes its new-wave direction with a hook designed to lodge itself immediately in the ear. Atmospheric synthesizers spread across the arrangement while Zedolik’s thundering baritone rises above them, channeling Bowie through a repeated vocal phrase that feels closer to a public chant than an intimate confession. The song turns memory into something immense and communal, giving private recollection the scale of a crowded room singing the same words back at the stage. Sympathy‘s character falls somewhere between the grave authority of the Sisters of Mercy and the brisk rhythmic snap of the English Beat, with dark guitar and keyboard textures carried forward by an unexpectedly nimble pop current. At its center sits the album’s bluntest conclusion, “Sympathy is never free,” a line delivered less as wounded revelation than settled economic fact. The compact Reckoning strips away much of the surrounding machinery for a sparse ballad that recalls Peter Murphy’s theatrical poise and the Gun Club’s scorched romanticism. Zedolik leaves greater space around the vocal, allowing each phrase to land with the weight of an overdue admission. Together, the three songs frame Existor as a record about accounting in every sense: years spent, affection owed, compromises concealed, debts carried forward, and personal myths steadily losing value under the pressure of experience. Existor is severe, catchy, and suspicious of every emotional transaction. It leaves the listener wondering who benefits, who pays, and whether the receipt was printed before the conversation even began. Listen to the album below, and order it here. Existor by Zeu Released through Wilkes-Barre imprint Everything Evaporated, Existor is ZEU’s eighth full-length album, which means this private factory has been running for years while much of the music business was busy inventing new names for layoffs. Mike McTague’s artwork gives the project a face, as Zedolik helms the controls, building pop songs from accumulated experience and present-tense unease. The result feels built for headphones, highways, and anyone who distrusts a cheerful invoice. Follow Zeu: Spotify Instagram The post “Sympathy Is Never Free” — Pennsylvania Post-Punk Artist ZEU Unveils “Existor” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
