items.tags: art sound art contemporary music improvisation
items.excerpt: 会期：2026/06/23～2026/10/04 会場：アーティゾン美術館［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://www.artizon.museum/exhibition_sp/sottsass2026/ 20世紀イタリアデザインの巨匠といわれるエットレ・ソットサスが、デザイナー集団「メンフィス」を結成してからもう40年以上が経つ。にもかかわらず、ポストモダンと評されたメンフィスが世界に与えた影響力は未だ計り知れず、これを超える思想性の高いデザイナーや集団は、その後も現われていない。むしろ、時代は再びモダンデザインという守りへ向かっているような気がしてならないのである。そうした意味で、本展はいまの世の中に対しても強烈なメッセージを残し得るに違いない。 「エットレ・ソットサス」展示風景 ©Yuya Furukawa 本展は日本初のソットサスの大規模回顧展であるとともに、アーティゾン美術館にとっては初のデザイン展として話題を集めている。同館を運営する公益財団法人石橋財団は、近年、デザイン分野の作品収集に注力し、中でもソットサスの初期から晩年におよぶコレクションを100点以上抱えるに至った
items.body: 会期：2026/06/23～2026/10/04 会場：アーティゾン美術館［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://www.artizon.museum/exhibition_sp/sottsass2026/ 20世紀イタリアデザインの巨匠といわれるエットレ・ソットサスが、デザイナー集団「メンフィス」を結成してからもう40年以上が経つ。にもかかわらず、ポストモダンと評されたメンフィスが世界に与えた影響力は未だ計り知れず、これを超える思想性の高いデザイナーや集団は、その後も現われていない。むしろ、時代は再びモダンデザインという守りへ向かっているような気がしてならないのである。そうした意味で、本展はいまの世の中に対しても強烈なメッセージを残し得るに違いない。 「エットレ・ソットサス」展示風景 ©Yuya Furukawa 本展は日本初のソットサスの大規模回顧展であるとともに、アーティゾン美術館にとっては初のデザイン展として話題を集めている。同館を運営する公益財団法人石橋財団は、近年、デザイン分野の作品収集に注力し、中でもソットサスの初期から晩年におよぶコレクションを100点以上抱えるに至ったという。幅広い分野の美術作品を所蔵する同館が、デザイン分野に目を向けた際、最も注目したのがソットサスの作品だったという点は興味深い。言い換えれば、美術の文脈でも十分に語れる作品だったということだろう。 「エットレ・ソットサス」展示風景 ©Yuya Furukawa 「エットレ・ソットサス」展示風景 ©Yuya Furukawa ソットサスがデザイナーとして歩んできた時代は、そのまま戦後のイタリア史および世界史と重なる。戦前にトリノ工科大学で学位を取得後、第二次世界大戦従軍を経て、1950年代からプロダクトや家具のデザインに本格的に携わるようになるからだ。彼の初期代表作は、何といってもオリベッティ社の真っ赤なタイプライター「ヴァレンタイン」である。本展は回顧展ということもあり、このように初期から晩年に向かってソットサスの来歴や作品を紹介する内容となっていた。インドを旅して影響を受けた東洋美術や、病床で描いた「トーテム」シリーズのドローイング、また数々のメタファーを表現したモノクロ写真シリーズなど、メンフィス結成に至るまでの経緯が手に取るようにわかり、彼の思想や作品に対する理解が進んだ。ソットサスからすればモダンデザインを考えることは容易いが、ポストモダン──すなわち「デザインとは何か」を哲学的に問い続けることほど難しいものはなかったのだろう。もちろん、デザインの基本姿勢は人々の暮らしや社会をより良くすることだ。しかし、その概念があまりに凝り固まってはいやしないか。ソットサスが生涯をかけて挑んだ活動にこそ、我々の頭を柔軟に解きほぐすヒントが隠れているように思う。 「エットレ・ソットサス」展示風景 ©Yuya Furukawa 鑑賞日：2026/06/30（火）

items.body: Grief is a universal experience that no one can truly be prepared for, and one that each of us inhabits differently, in ways we are unable to control or predict. Written for Paula Ďurinová’s film Lapilli, Petra Hermanova‘s soundtrack follows an exploration of death through stones, caves and volcanic landscapes, asking how the physical world absorbs and preserves traces of loss. The title refers to the fragments of rock ejected during a volcanic eruption—small stones suspended between destruction and renewal—and Hermanová’s music inhabits that same uncertain territory, poised between fragility and endurance. The opening suite, “Five Stages”, moves at a measured pace, every gesture carrying its full weight without ever tipping into emotional excess. Rather than illustrating the five stages of grief to which the title presumably alludes, the music creates a contemplative space in which listeners are left to negotiate that process for themselves, offering emotional cues without ever prescribing a response. Pieces such as “Outcome (Massives)” and “Soft Void” shift the focus towards resonance, silence and the physical behaviour of sound itself. Broken autoharps, their cracked strings given one final voice, merge with the film’s environmental soundscape until it becomes difficult to distinguish music from water droplets, stone or air. Each sound seems pared back to its essence, as though carved from rock rather than composed. By degrees the textures thicken and subtle trajectories begin to emerge, most clearly in “The Cave”, before “Dusk, Breath” brings the work to a close, the organ lending the final moments a quiet, almost liturgical sense of resolution. If In Death’s Eyes confronted bereavement as an intimate human wound, Lapilli broadens that perspective, suggesting that grief belongs as much to landscapes and geological time as it does to ourselves. Rather than offering consolation, Hermanová creates a place where mourning is simply allowed to continue, carried by stone, air and the slow passage of time. In the following interview conducted via email Petra Hermanova elaborates on her production process. Both In Death’s Eyes, your previous album and Lapilli are deeply concerned with death, grief, and transformation, but they seem to approach those themes from different angles. In In Death’s Eyes, death often appears as an intimate, almost bodily presence, whereas Lapilli explores loss through rocks, caves, minerals, and geological time. Did working on Paula Ďurinová’s film change the way you think about death? Did it shift your focus from personal grief toward a broader relationship between mortality, landscape, and material transformation? The way I think about death was most significantly changed by experiencing the death of a loved one. Anything that came afterwards was more damage control. Paula and I went through a grieving process around the same time, and we also worked on our debuts in parallel. When I was in the Merseburg Cathedral recording organ for my album, Paula was descending deep inside of cave systems to film for her documentary, and we kept texting each other photographs of these incredible spaces. They were profound experiences and I remember quite clearly that life made sense again in those moments, the pain was transmuted. I tried to think about working on my album as a way of contributing to the canon of music dealing with human mortality, but it still ended up being a very personal work. I came to a different understanding with Lapilli. Having been invited to write music for someone else’s reckoning with death, I got to observe a separate grieving process. Suddenly there were different associations, metaphors and coping mechanisms in place, and this was a much stronger departure from the personal to the universal. The autoharp plays a central role in both works, yet its function feels different. On In Death’s Eyes, it often acts as the voice of the individual sufferer, standing in tension with the transcendence of the pipe organ. On Lapilli, the autoharp seems to become part of the landscape itself, with its detuned and deteriorating strings echoing caves, stone, and erosion. How did your relationship with the instrument evolve between these two projects, and what drew you to its increasingly fragile and material qualities? Autoharp is a matter close to my heart, maybe more of an obsession. I always feel a bit sad that I can only ever bring two with me while I’m performing because they are all so different. Writing music for film is more free in this aspect, and so my first thought was to use the broken autoharps in my collection, the ones that I don’t dare to restring and tune properly, because they’re too fragile, too cracked. There is an analogy somewhere in there about the possibilities of someone who feels fragile and broken but still would like to be useful. I thought a lot about instruments that are no longer played and just lay somewhere, completely mute. Even one of my main instruments hung on a wall somewhere in Spandau for decades, before I got it. So it was about seeing what kind of sounds can be still coaxed out of these “dead” autoharps, and this couldn’t be further away from how I usually write music. There is a peculiar sports event called the Autoharp Toss in which participants of a musical gathering compete in tossing an autoharp beyond repair as far as they can. Instead of that, I took these autoharps and recorded their swan songs. Lapilli is the soundtrack to “a soft film about hard matter” and the liner notes ask how rocks, pebbles, and mountains die. The music often feels suspended between human memory and geological time, as if grief is being measured against processes far older than ourselves. When composing the music, were you trying to sonify the landscape itself, or were the sounds primarily a way of reflecting the emotional journey of the film’s narrator through loss? Lapilli is now a music release, but in the film it exists alongside the sound design Paula worked on with the composer and musician Agnese Menguzzato. In places they are so intertwined, that it can be difficult to distinguish what is music and what is sound design—in the caves, the pluck of an autoharp string may as well be the sound of a water drop. We talked at great lengths about all these scenes and what they represent. I am a very visual person, so while it sometimes felt a little bit like looking for the sound of the landscape, or of all these various geological processes the landscapes undergo, most often we were working in more abstract terms, superimposing sonic parallels onto fragments of text or mental states that informed these scenes. As the film moves through its stages, the instrumentation develops a narrative also, and the broken autoharps are at first accompanied, and then slowly replaced with the steady breath of an organ. In In Death’s Eyes, lyrics played a crucial role in articulating grief, uncertainty, and the tension between spiritual and earthly forms of consolation. Lapilli, by contrast, communicates almost entirely through instrumental sound, texture, and space. Did working on a film allow you to express things that language couldn’t? How different was it to construct meaning through timbre, resonance, and silence rather than through words and song? By the time I started composing for Lapilli, I had been working with the theme of death for almost two years. I saw it as an opportunity to extend and inhabit the same space with similar means, but with a very different set of constraints and reasons for them. In my practice, the usual starting point is silence. I then fill the silence with as little as I can, or as much as I want to. This time, the starting point was an already emotionally saturated image with an equally charged narration, so I had to construct different poetic principles for this work. How much can I add without overloading this moment? How sparse can I go—and will it still be music then? Previously I hadn’t considered making purely instrumental music, so this was pivotal, it opened a new channel for me. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Explorer is a richly detailed journey through melodic ambient electronics and progressive textures, where Parallel Worlds transforms the mystery, beauty, and endless motion of deep space into nine immersive sonic voyages. Our journeys into space remind us to look up and stay curious Explorer by Parallel Worlds   Strange prog rock tinged ambient electronic music that captures much of the experience of being in space, each track is a unique haunting melody, a jeweled glass music box to explore. Space travel is glamorous. The feeling of floating and bouncing around without gravity captures much of the imagination, there are nine journeys into the dark infinity of space, covered with distant star clusters and galaxies. I hear a very idiosyncratic language of unmistakable electronic beeps, tocks and ticks, constructed of weaving intricate nimble rapid cyclic interactions. A clockwork of multiple interacting moving parts, with engaging craftsmanship and a polished presentation. Here on Earth, our journeys into space remind us to look up and stay curious. World creating music makes cosmic galactic travel go smoothly, the machines are built to run forever, in pursuit of intimate lunar mysteries, to break through the light barriers, and search for life among the stars. Our universe is a wide and wonderful place. The cover design is by LoMo, and the sound was mastered by Lorenzo Montana, all Parallel Worlds Explorer tracks were composed, arranged and produced by Bakis Sirros during 2025 using Eurorack modular (including modules by Qu-Bit, Synthesis Technology, Make Noise, Instruo, Xaoc Devices, Frap Tools, Doepfer, 4ms company, Noise Engineering, Buchla Tiptop Audio, Befaco, Neuzeit, Strymon, Steady State Fate, Cosmotronic, Hexinverter, Industrial Music Electronics, Endorphin.es, Behringer and others), Analogue Systems RS-Integrator modular, Roland System-8, korg Prologue, Wavestate, Opsix, SQ64, MS2000R, ASM Hydrasynth, Novation Peak, Kodamo EssenceFM mk2, Yamaha TG77, Waldorf Microwave, Behringer Model-D. Opening with a melody from outer space, bearing a melodic easy tempo, mysterious, fast and pleasant, “Bendophonic” (7:15) builds into upbeat frisky and color-rich flocks of electronic birds, the speed of lots of voices combines as one message, slowly things are starting to get dark. The bright blue sky quickly turns pitch black as we climb higher. The orchestra awakens in a new galaxy :: The bass brings us in slow and low, followed with electronic snaps and buzzy drones, the layers build, a keyboard sets up the framework and away we go, “Phase” (5:18). Tricky percussion percolates in like cocoa, I hear sinister steps behind me, casting long gloomy shadows haunting desolate and dark, I am enjoying the ride, now it ends. The orchestra awakens in a new galaxy, “Still Unknown” (4:26), always calling out,  seeking a signal in return, forming a jammin’ bass percussion line revealing visions from outer space, an old ceremonial contemplative ritual that takes centuries to repeat. Perhaps a strange question hangs in the melody. Engines shut off and you instantly float, moving in several dimensions like flying. Opening like an almost forgotten television series, “Persistence” (5:17) brings lots of moving parts that fit together and create a cyclic pattern that evolves and adds new dimensions as it goes. The immense spiral gyre comes overflowing into the shoreline, with lots of details and layered repetition, humans are learning how to live and work in space. “Patience” (6:30) starts slow, a spider web of moonlight, playing on spiral glass bowls dark with roses and silver, genty struck ringing bell glass objects, a dance finish, very sparse and swooning in places. Astronauts often spend extended amounts of time in space, always to pave the way for even longer, future exploration missions. After riding across the night sky forever, “Fullmoon” (7:02) paints a picture. The moonlight now has more colors than just silver, but the picture started with silver, honoring the children of the night. Here there are all kinds of colors and a choppy moist energetic beat holding strong all through the track. It seems that they come from the sky, with complex weaving layers of beat and melodic themes being ground quite finely. These repeating cycles add new beeps and buzzing strangesounds that change, new strangesounds held on the same rhythm as one flow, slowly turning in the hall of mirrors, “Soundwise” (5:17). We are making some dreamy dark distance as the machine beats and bips along, weaving its patterns with plenty of mysterious electronic atmospheric details. With many a light-year to go tonight, tonight feels different. “Tonight” (5:22) breaks out with chimes followed by a strong bass, a triumphant journey into percussive synergy, with some tight jams and electronic voices answering and calling. Now I hear little dancing robots with period costumes, perhaps telling another story about another night in another place and it fits tonight here at last. The climax, “Octo” (7:08) opens with a question posed by an electronic voice. I do not know what it is saying in the icy darkness. I hear a buzzy beat box click in, which takes the ever cycling helix pattern in a strong new direction, into another new hall of mirrors. Somehow, midway things drop out. We drift for a moment, but ultimately the ride continues forever, nothing changes anymore, we just cycle and look into infinity all around.​ Explorer is available on Neo Ouija. [Bandcamp] Explorer by Parallel WorldsThe post Parallel Worlds :: Explorer (Neo Ouija) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: This Daily Discovery isn’t the usual kind… These features normally just point you towards something worth hearing and watching; this one also asks you to help. Alice in WonderBand are Ana Vrbaški and Marko Dinjaški, a Serbian duo who have been together on stage and off it for 28 years. They live out near the Fruška Gora National Park in the north of the country and make all their music from the body: hands clapping and snapping, feet stamping the floor, chests and thighs slapped for the low end, tongues and mouth clicks filling the gaps, Ana at the piano, Marko on didgeridoo and darbuka, and the tunes carried in their voices. Most of what they sing began as Balkan folk song, which they take apart and rebuild in the odd, uneven rhythms of the region. On 11 July, Ana was seriously injured as a passenger in a car accident, and she now faces a long period of treatment and rehabilitation. The couple had a full summer of concerts ahead of them, and all of it has fallen through, their income with it. Friends have set up a fundraiser to help meet the cost of her care and steady the months to come. You can donate HERE, or give directly through PayPal at THIS LINK. If a donation isn’t possible, sharing it helps just as much. The song in the video is one of theirs. “Dokonanje”, which roughly means being idle, is a track from their new album, The Courage to be Afraid. They recorded it in May with their daughter, Alisa Dinjaški, alongside “Vrbice, Vrbo Zeljena”, a Gorani song from Kosovo. It is an old piece, written almost twenty years ago, and the words still read like a motto. “Dokonanje” means being idle, but the song argues the opposite: the refrain insists “We’re not being idle”, then lists the digging, mowing and carrying of water that fills the day. The video was filmed at Slovenia’s Kavč festival, a travelling event that for ten years has staged concerts in living rooms, bookshops and town squares under Matija Solce. Alice in WonderBand played the Fragmenti bookshop in Kranj. This year Ana and Marko, together with Julia Lewandowska and Łukasz Malok from CISI, also brought Slavyk to life, a quartet that sets Silesian and Serbian folk traditions to English lyrics. Their debut, 11 Songs of Love and Suffering, was released this June on CPL Music. If you can, stand with Ana and Marko by giving or sharing THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Alice in Wonderband – Dokonanje (Live @ Kavč Festival, Fragmenti Bookstore) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Rising Appalachia‘s “Chance at Wholesome” is a folk song about a specific type of man: the one who performs devotion and withholds it, who lights a fire and vanishes before it catches, who offers the shape of love without the substance. Leah Song and Chloe Smith sing him down in close harmony. The sisters were born in Atlanta and have long been based in Asheville, in the North Carolina mountains, where they took up clawhammer banjo and fiddle in their twenties after a childhood of classical piano and weekends at fiddle conventions across the Southeast. Twenty years of Rising Appalachia has carried them from busking in New Orleans to Red Rocks and NPR’s Tiny Desk, all of it self-managed and independently financed. The group runs on sibling harmony, banjo and fiddle over world percussion, with David Brown on upright bass and baritone guitar, Duncan Wickel on fiddle and cello and Biko Casini on drums. The same lineup plays “Chance at Wholesome”, the sisters’ harmony carrying the verses. “Chance at Wholesome” is the second single from Trade My Troubles, a sixteen-track album due on 2 October, bookended by a traditional Irish traveller song and an Appalachian fiddle tune. The US autumn tour opens with two nights at Pisgah Brewing in Black Mountain, the band’s annual Hurricane Helene commemoration shows, then runs through the Southeast to Moab Folk Festival before finishing in New York. Stream “Chance at Wholesome” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Rising Appalachia – Chance at Wholesome appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — More than a catharsis, it feels like a descent into the depths, built upon guitar and bass, yet the Minimoog introduces a different sensation that gives the track lift and elevates the musical vision of "Catastasis," the opening song on Elder's seventh album.Two guitars. Two keyboards. A composition with an epic scope that differs radically from that of classic heavy metal. It leans closer to Rush, creating the impression that every head-banging, aggressive passage... culminates in another that tears open portals to a different dimension, prompting a different kind of head-nodding altogether. Next comes a chorus led by Behrang Alavi, followed by a succession of riffs that constantly outdo one another. It is orchestral heavy metal without an actual orchestra, a sound that is symphonic and grand, yet loses none of its power or even its aggressive edge."Endless Return" moves at a breakneck pace that offers no respite; Behrang Alavi handles the vocals here, while the two guitars display virtuosity, building a powerful, and highly original, melody in tandem with the drums. The track's progressive character is further enhanced when the Mellotron and bass kick in. Bass-driven instrumental sections featuring guitar runs evoke the best of Rush, yet the entry of the synthesizer rounds out the perfect sonic picture the band has crafted. It is evident that they prioritized not only playing with skill and intensity but also composing original, vibrant pieces."Coalescence" gives the impression that they can't quite contain the momentum they've unleashed?reminiscent of the opening of "Close to the Edge", but then a more meditative passage with Mellotron kicks in. Just as I'm reminded of King Crimson, a highly original section emerges that doesn't call to mind anyone else, only Elder themselves. It possesses a psychedelic and almost jazzy sensibility, without ever explicitly crossing into that genre, driven by a melody that instantly hooks you. It's as if they've captured the best of both worlds: harmony and power, plus that dash of surprise that keeps you glued to the music."Merged in Dreams - Ne Plus Ultra" has a drawn-out opening that almost lulls one into a state of lethargy... the album title, Innate Passage, reminded me of that Kafka story about the door made just for us, one we didn't dare step through, only to see it close as the end approached... leaving us to realize the truth too late. Everything lies within us, and sometimes something awakens it, acting as a catalyst; I like to think of the object on the cover as such a catalyst, something each of us can use for ourselves. In fact, the music itself is exactly that.Nicholas DiSalvo sings and plays guitar alongside drum breaks that recall the wilder moments of Gong's You, building a pyramid of distortion that suddenly collapses, as if made of sand, revealing that what we had been witnessing was merely a desert mirage. When the two guitars join forces, it feels like an explosive finale, with playing as rapid as Steve Howe's during his classic era.Then comes a keyboard sequence that feels almost electronic; when the guitar and drums kick in, it resembles a beating heart, racing at times. This leads into the closing track, "The Purpose," which revisits that electro-rock vibe, with notes that lend the song a sense of maturity. Innate Passage does not disappoint; instead, it fuels that inner fire, that light that never goes out.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — A radical shift awaited the Swedish band between their first album and this one, titled Tv�, which consists of just two lengthy tracks; the first, "G�ngl�t fr�n Vintergatan," lacks the complexity and density of its predecessor. It is only around the halfway mark that the organ introduces Eastern-tinged melodies with a 1960s psychedelic vibe; Celtic influences are present, as are echoes of Jethro Tull, evident not just in the flute work but in the composition itself.Midway through, the organ takes an even more prominent role, combining with the percussion to evoke the kind of soliloquies found in The Doors' music; however, the frenetic energy that linked the band's debut to the likes of Van der Graaf Generator or early Santana is missing here. Mikael �desj� delivers fine guitar work during a sort of jam session that nonetheless retains a distinctly Celtic feel."Kung Bores dans" is the album's second track, featuring organ work that, this time around, truly embarks on the anticipated journey, though it gives the impression of being a bit drawn-out without offering many fresh ideas. Instrumentally, it is flawless, and the transitions between sections are skillfully executed, handled with subtlety and shifting modos, at times even maintaining a tense, suspense-filled calm before the dramatic intrigue resumes. On this track, the guitar work is somewhat reminiscent of the Pink Floyd sound found on "Echoes" (from the album Meddle).Around the halfway mark, the organ and guitar take center stage, performing duets and sounding a bit like Camel on their debut album. Towards the end, the organ notes drop to a lower register, taking on a somewhat Canterbury-esque feel, and are impeccably accompanied by drummer Tim Wallander, who was making his debut on this record. The finale gains power and a certain darkness that suits it well, lending a depth that the Swedish forest setting had been lacking.

items.body: Review by ianjferris@gmail.com — I will make no reference in this review to Volume One - The Shorts. That is for another time. This album, Volume Two of The Way We Walk - The Longs, is a very strong album. It packs some real power into its 70 minutes, with no weak moments. Now I know that some people will decry the fact that the older material (particularly the stuff from the "Peter Gabriel era") is stripped back to the bone and all included in a soft rock style medley of some nineteen and a half minutes. But lets face facts here. This older material comes from about 20 years previously. At the time this album was recorded in 1992, it was natural that Genesis (or any band still going strong after so many years) would cut back on the older stuff, in order to play their more contemporaneous material for that more modern crowd, a lot of whom may have still been in nappies (or diapers in the USA) or who may not have been born at all when the older material was first released! But what they do play here from the 1970's, in this 1992 live setting, is delivered with impressive power, with precision and not a little expertise. But it's not played in a "rough and raw" way. It's played with an air of accomplisment by the original authors/composers, who are now more accomplished musicians themselves. In fact, the original 1970's studio albums, absolutely brilliant as they are, just can't compete with this live delivery of the 1990's. The four long songs from the 1980's and 1990's - Driving The Last Spike, Domino, Fading Lights and Home By The Sea are also delivered with a lot more panache and power than their respective versions on the studio albums. These are the versions that define these Progressive Rock monsters for me. Yes, I do like the originals but these live renditions are my favourites.I saw Genesis playing live on the Duke Tour, as they were in the midst of transitioning from their 1970's Progressive Rock rooted style into their Art/Progressive Pop pomp of the 1980's and 1990's. They were magnificent back then, in 1980. unfortunately I just didn't get to see them on their The Way We Walk Tour in 1992. But based on this album, "The Longs" CD, I can only imagine that it must have been electrifying for the audience! I suppose that I really should now declare that I'm a committed and dedicated fan of Genesis, right through all phases and incarnations of the band. And thats why, even though this review is written fully in accordance with Progarchives Guidelines, I can't restrict my award for this album to 4 stars. I just can't do that. The album is too good for that. It's just as good as all their other live albums, from all the different eras over the decades. So I'm proceeding upwards and I'm giving the album the full 5 stars.

items.body: Review by Naida Regent — Listen up! If the stars are lit, it means? they burn too brightly for this world. Unfortunately, the genius "psychedelic" wrote a little, but his works are immortal. Good works, which include a unique transparent sound, which is typical, however, for many English performers and bands. Transparent, like the air of their homeland, inhaled by the instrument and blown into our ears. Some of the compositions are English fantasy fairy tales (Matilda Mother, The Gnome, Scarecrow), and the main action is a great cosmic journey through which this "star gentleman" travels. He gives the light of these stars to us and his group, who set off on a more distant earthly journey. And he stayed on the other side of the moon. My assessment is not accidental. I'd like to thank you for the innovation of transparent sound and cosmically ethereal vocals, born (not in pain). The only band, in my opinion, where there is such a combination is Yes. But that's another story.

items.body: Review by Naida Regent — The album "An Ambassador in Bonds" is as good (and atmospheric) as the first one. The same turns and twists, the same "Petersburg" mood of the Silver Age of Russian poetry. Poetic images are felt in every note. If the poets of this era could clothe their words in music, then it would be just like that. The alternation of light and dark sections of musical constructions reminds me of Russian periods in general, without which they do not exist. Either wandering in search of the meaning of existence, then the joy of finding it run like a red thread through the tracks and lead the audience out of any dead end that prevents them from reaching the heights of flaming optimism. Listen to this! And you will have an even greater desire to learn, to work and to make yourself. Further wishes to this collective: "move" their works towards symphonic ones. And there it is not far from ready-made requiems.

items.body: Review by Naida Regent — The album "Narrow is the Road" is more coherent than the previous two. It feels the spirit of the present time, the ongoing difficult events that have affected Ukraine and Russia in 2022. In every note, one can feel personal involvement of the performers and the transfer of this to the listeners. "He who has ears to hear, let him hear." This gospel saying best fits the theme of the album. There are fewer things that are heavy in perception and in mood than on previous albums; rather there is a certain mood that awakens all the best inside the human mind, inside our understanding on the path of searching for the truth. The titles of the compositions are also united by one goal - the awakening of reason and mercy. Here is a musical example that shows that it is possible to speak about difficult things in a very simple language. It is not difficult to be a humanist and it is not too late to become; while you're still alive, do it faster so the world doesn't fall apart. The composer Jenkins has an oratorio titled "A Mass for Peace". The album "Narrow is the Road" can safely be called its continuation.

items.body: Review by Naida Regent — After listening to "Daybreaking Live" album I had discovered for myself new Roz Vitalis, although previously I listened to this band time and time again. At the present moment compositions are perceived as more mature and "grow" with musicians both physically and mentally. The sound became more heavy and dense. Due to more heavy guitar and more heavy rhythm-section "approach" of the band comes closer to progressive metal. But, at the same time, Roz Vitalis's style remains true to oneself and recognizable. Evidently, the group wants to take from prog a little bit of everything and, at the same time, to be distinctive and original. As before, there are baroque-and-medieval motives. In "Nepsis" and "Psalm 6" motives of dancing heaviness transform into tranquil transcendence. In each composition there are memorable and hit melodies. "Mother of All Rain" remains the most melodic one. The flute sounds remarkably, but I would like to hear more winds like in "The Hidden Man of the Heart" album. In general, in the future it would be better to increase quantity of wind instruments (clarinet, saxophone, trumpet, French Horn). The same wishes concern use of string instruments (violin, cello, double bass, viola). The main recommendation is to move to symphonic style of music.

items.body: Review by Naida Regent — I hear a voice from a beautiful Canterbury far-away? It plunged me into memories of seemingly unlike each other things ? 1) of course, the bands of "Canterbury periods", and 2) music of the Soviet time ? for films, tales, etc. Now then ? it would seem evident ? Russia and England are similar in spontaneously natural musical feeling. This is even so. I hope that this experience will not be lost, and we will hear its numerous incarnations further ? everywhere. The album abounds in "natural", that is, sounds-of-nature-imitating instruments. There are not only classical "multi-orchestral" opuses, but also sounds of raindrops, knock of twigs on roof, and other spontaneously planetary sonorities. As well as we can hear typical for this group "entries" into the other countries ? for example, Japan (tracks 3 and 4), England (tracks 7 ? 9), Spain, etc. And that is good! Requests ? I would like to listen to more depth and precision of each instrument's sound. In all other respects, Patience of Hope (my nickname Naida in Russian almost implies Hope in English) has been satisfied. I rate 5, first of all, for "primary nature" of the stuff.

items.album: ROZ VITALIS Dedication To BigNick (RIO/Avant-Prog, 2025)

items.body: Review by Naida Regent — This album is the first release in the history of the project dedicated to a specific person, alas, who left us, the talented producer Nikolai Bogaichuk. I heard in this album a reverent appeal to the addressee, echoes of the past, good, bright communication. The musicians seem to be continuing a dialogue with a person who already exists in another reality, and he responds to them. It's as if they can hear each other in the musical canvas of the works. A roll call of instruments is created - keyboards, wind instruments, etc. The first tracks are like the intro to a peculiar symphony of mystical roll call. The middle is active, vital, because a person lives in us as long as the memory of him is alive. And the ending is an epilogue, completing the journey on earth and looking into another future, an unknown world. Everyone "applies" the ease of perception to herself/himself. Everyone carries the weight of loss within herself/himself. When listening to this album, the effect is "opposite", where grief should not be boundless, and happiness should not be fleeting. It is not the first time that we have heard Ivan Rozmainsky's symphonic "approach", which is always inherent in him, and we hope that he will develop this to the level of the immortal classics.

items.body: Review by Naida Regent — In the cold Spring time I was very sad. I felt blue due to the dominance of musical culture promoted by mass media. I had made decision to listen to new album of the band which is known and loved by me for a long time because of the originality. The album "The Hidden Man of the Heart" is much darker than previous, "Lavoro d'Amore", but in the process of listening to the feeling of depression does not appear. If to take technical sides that this album sounds more professionally than previous ones. If to make comparisons with other artists then it the band "combines in one flacon" early Pink Floyd, King Crimson, and ELP. It also reminds exercises of Robert Fripp and Brian Eno. If to give characteristics of the style then it is progressive-psychedelic-electronic format with elements of German classical music, for example, Wagner. Recommended to listen to for those who want quickly to move from the state of sadness to the state of joy.

items.body: Review by Naida Regent — The album QNQF has a more expressed harmonic-melodic component of the musical canvas of the band titled Roz Vitalis. It's like a narrative author's work, a fantastic epic for the film. The prologue, climax and epilogue of the narrative are clearly audible. We read music like a book, the letters of the notes will sound in our memory for a long time. The echoes of low whistle, flute and clarinet sound very natural and spontaneous. The harpsichord adds the harmonic thought of the Renaissance to the general background. The eastern rubab and doira in track 8 are an echo of the desert. It is pleasant to listen to the album in any mood. It both soothes and evokes a bright sadness at times that are pleasant for everyone to remember. For some, this is the period of childhood, for others - love for people and circumstances. This is a message to humanity in principle. It does not have to be pathos-heroic, it also happens to be lyrically romantic, like the next wonderful creation of this collective given to us.

items.body: Review by OlyaBeginner — Listening to this tribute album felt like walking through familiar landscapes that suddenly open in a new light. Each track keeps the spirit of Depeche Mode, but also brings its own emotional depth, hidden meanings, and soft discoveries. I let the sound guide me through feelings, as if I was travelling inside both the past and something renewed.But Not Tonight The atmosphere is gentle and heartfelt. From the very beginning, the melody breathes sincerity. It feels touching and emotional, as if light itself wants to comfort. There is a sense of development ? inspiration to move forward, to grow, to reach for something bright. The composition gives hope and tenderness at the same time.World Full of Nothing The entrance is very light, flowing like air. The vocal creates the sensation of flight, of being above everything ordinary. Then comes the acceleration ? like the process of reaching a goal or realization. Finally, calmness returns, a peaceful landing after movement. The track teaches to breathe again after striving.The Things You Said This version is more lyrical than the original. It feels deeply emotional and intimate. The voice sounds almost magical, creating the feeling of being submerged into someone's secret thoughts. It's like a quiet dialogue between hearts that once knew sorrow and still remember beauty.Blue Dress Here appears the image of the road, the path. The rhythm invites movement, but also reflection. The vocal creates a romantic atmosphere, full of warmth and longing. It's not about distance, but about closeness ? about walking together through the unknown.Sibeling A mysterious night sky opens above the listener. There are stars, strange signals, maybe echoes of something cosmic. A quiet unease lives inside the sound ? a feeling of something unresolved, of searching. Then comes realization, acceptance, and a decision to move on. The music calms down as if peace was finally found in the middle of mystery.Enjoy the Silence The atmosphere here is magical and light. The voice gives softness, almost like silk on the surface of air. Gradually the sound grows stronger, more intense ? as if emotions expand beyond control. Then the voice returns again to bring comfort, to balance. The ending carries the listener away into clouds, into quiet joy. It's the emotional peak of the album ? a nine-minute journey through dream, reflection, and inner freedom.Together these compositions reveal the hidden depths of the familiar songs. The band develops the melodic foundation of Depeche Mode into something renewed ? sensitive, emotional, and thoughtful. What once seemed simple now opens with unexpected power. This tribute doesn't imitate; it transforms. It reminds that music lives not only in sound, but also in our personal discoveries and inner movements.

items.body: Review by OlyaBeginner — I won't describe the quality of musical instruments, I will just tell you, what feelings this work has evoked. Day breaking makes you feel despair, acceptance, peace. Your thoughts are being stopped and focus on the fact where and when you are. This composition makes you accept life as it is, the rules it has.Fountain makes you remember about hurt, tears you have in your life but it reminds that there is always hope that everything is gonna be ok.Se camminiamo Nella Luce evokes anxiety, fear and again hope. It tells you we can overcome difficult period, but we should try and work in order to contribute to making things better.Premonition - starting gradually, like growing. Brutal, strong and determined, with pauses to respite and rethink. Maybe you were doing something wrong. Maybe there are important things you weren't paying attention.Walking - is brutal too, changing to cute. Sometimes people need to stop being strong and show their weaknesses, have some rest and after that again get into a diligent rhythm of life in order to get what you want.Wides - the idea of taking an oath of fighting unfairness and cruelty runs through the entire album. Here in particular. In the beginning you don't know what to do, maybe feel confused. But then you realise that the only right thing is you never gonna give up. Bustle of hard work will fix troubles. But of course you have to take breaks when you feel tiredness, which is pleasant. You keep doing your thing following your oath.The man whose wings were cut off - hurt and shock, confused and uncertain, sadness and brutal.Beautifulness - admiration with beautifulness, but this beautifulness consists of kindness and love for other people.Nocturne - makes you remember people you stop being close with and feel thankful for all time you spent together and unforgettable experience they gave you. You are just thankful that they were in your life. Light sadness and love fill the soul, even it's not mutual.So this album has the great power to make a listener feel a bunch of emotions and immerses him/her in a different sorts of atmosphere. Sometimes it comforts, sometimes it inspires to go forward.

items.body: Review by Archisorcerus — I discovered this obscure gem in the autumnal times of the year 2024, and got immediately hooked by the music here. This project has offered only this jewel as of yet, however its mastermind "Lord Vrajitor" (and more aliases with the word vrajitor) still seems busy with some other projects, most of which, methinks, are within the black metal domains. Don't get outright frightened, this album of him/theirs (theirs, because he is not the sole musician in the album) is pure prog rock. Or not so pure... At least, it has nothing to do with metal, let alone the notorious black metal. Or is there a sinister connection?.. Haha. Vrajitor means wizard/sorcerer in the Romanian language. Too romantic, isn't it. Ha-ha! - As you can guess from my username, I'm quite interested in such "names", and I already had learned what vrajitor means before even hearing about this band.Well... This is really a solid album, I think. Not too avant-garde, though, unlike its label suggests. Vrajitor seems like a young guy, and perhaps in time he can sharpen his blade and cut through the vines which can block the path to achieve some real authentic originality. This really requires some maturity in general. I didn't want to say that this album is not original, I just cannot hear anything that makes me say "Wow, I've never heard anything like this before!" - Yet, this is a really atmospheric output that has a great soul, besides its musical solidity; which is an invaluable asset. It can sound nostalgic, magickal, occultic (and so forth), and the record is really of high quality in general.Though there are some problems in it, if not major. Firstly, the "fade-out trick" was used thrice, two of which are not okay for me by any means. Secondly, in the 4th track's 0:28 second, I really hear a timing error in drums. No matter how many times I listen to the album (which as of yet should be 20-30 times), that timing inaccuracy still disturbs me, though slightly. Normally I could have overlooked it, but in the rest of the album we hear some flawless musicianship, so that little timing thing really disturbs me a bit. The crash hitting is a bit late there. Dunno if it is a deliberate artistic twist, which can be seen in prog rock, but I frankly get displeased by it. These 2 are all. I mean I have no other "complaints" concerning this truly impressive work.If Lord/Magus Vrajitor releases some other works with this band of his, I'd definitely get excited enough to check them out. His black metal stuff?.. I don't envision myself doing so. Mind you, I like me some black metal stuff, but they are really too scarce... Maybe this album of Vrajitor's Tenebrarium has no direct relation with black metal musically, but it seems to have an indirect one... This album is labeled as "dungeon funk" as well. I had never heard of such a genre before discovering this band/album. Presumably, it is kinda like the genre entitled dungeon synth, albeit not that dismal, conversely uplifting perhaps. Lord Vrajitor also has a dungeon synth past, as I read/know... Yeah, kinda the medievalesque "air" of dungeon synth is here, but without the toxic depressivity. Let the oceans of good spirits seep in! The connection here is that, dungeon synth has some ancient and very strong ties with black metal. In the genesis of the dungeon synth, there already was the nefarious black metal residing in the nightside of Eden, whispering some ominous incantations in dungeon synth's ears...4/5 stars. So, definitely recommended.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Recorded in four consecutive days at the end of August, 1973, at Dieter Dierks studio in Stommeln, it was then released by Bacillus Records in November. 1. "Kabisrain" (7:59) Eddy Marron plays solo baglama to open things up. Bowed bass, Super String synth, gongs, cymbals, and shakers come next. Retaining a Middle Eastern sound and feel as more instruments are exchanged/introduced (steel string acoustic guitar, drum kit cymbals and timpani), the band continues to extend that which feels more like an introduction well into the sixth minute--the song never really congealing into something substantial. Interesting but not even in the same ball park as the wonderful music that POPOL VUH had been doing for three years. (12.5/15)2. "Magika" (8:45) jumping straight into something like you might hear on a TONY WILLIAMS album, the trio of electric guitar and electric bass and rock drums revolves around Peter Giger's dynamic drum exhibition over the course of the first minute, then they pick up on a John McLaughlin riff, bend it and tweak it before flat-lining it into a percussive romp. The ensuing motif is almost minimalist in its subtle-yet-constantly changing polyrhythmic weave. The at the three-minute mark some guitar chords signal a change: one that is spacious, without forward motion, and very bluesy and free--with not a few moments reminding me of Jaco Pastorius-era Weather Report. In the second half of the fifth minute Reinhard starts up a bass riff that remains rather fixed and forward moving over which Peter continues his rhythmic show and Eddy shreds on his distorted Hendrix/Albrighton/Coryell way. Here I'm finding myself thinking more of Jack DeJohnette's early albums as band leader--his collaborations with John Abercrombie. Wonderful musicianship expressing a lot of wildly free-form energy. (17.75/20)3. "Light Shining Out Of Darkness" (3:13) a very satisfying Jazz-Rock Fusion tune with multiple guitar parts, acoustic and electric, and both bass and double bass playing over Peter Giger's laid back power drumming. The opening 12-string guitar work is awesome. (Is it the "Super String synth" making the accordion sound?) (9.125/10)4. "Time machine" (17:47) a STEVE TIBBETTS-like Mahavishnu barrage of guitar and sophisticated syncopated Jazz drumming open this for the opening minute before an interlude of Mellotron-like synth (the "Super String synth"?) and delicate and chromatically-melodic electric guitar note play takes over for about a minute. Then the Tibbetts/Mahavishnu motif returns to start things back up, now moving at the four minute mark into a smoother, forward moving bass, drums, and rhythm guitar groove over which Eddy continues to shred with his Mahavishnu-styled and -sounding lead guitar. Sad that they felt it necessary to use an ad nauseum repeating four-chord rock motif to lay beneath Eddy's guitar shredding over the course of the entire second half of the song! (30/35)Total Time: 37:44Yes, I can hear/feel the Mahavishnu Orchestra inspiration in Dzyan's sound and approach but they have none of the polish and structure of the MO.C/three stars; an album that definitely has Jazz-Rock Fusion energy but seems to be often quite lacking in terms of goals, form, or structure; it feels like a band of extraordinary musicians who only want to show how extraordinary they are, thereby eschewing the creation of memorable music.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Carmine Capasso is a young and ultra-talented guitarist, making quite a name for himself not only in the Italian prog community with The Trip and solo work but also globally. He teams up with the legendary early bassist of PFM. This is a live recording of a pan-Italian 2-year tour and features tracks from the above-mentioned bands as well as other pieces from Lucio Battisti, Ivan Graziani, Ennio Morricone, The Shadows, I Quelli, ELP and King Crimson. Piero Chifa handles bass and rhythm guitar, the drums handled by Jacopo Casadio and Guiseppe Sarno on keyboards. As a counterbalance to AI as well as over-produced sterile manufacture, the band chooses a raw, organic and no overdub presentation, capturing the true essence of live, and verifiable expression. The sugar is in the material and not in the coating. The set-list has three distinctive sections, the more personal material first, a slew of Italian oldies and then a stunning series of legendary covers that features a few tracks we all know and adore. The mood is set right from the onset with a couple of pieces from his solo album, Carmine getting to shine on the terrific "Neve Nera" (Black Snow), a mid-tempo romantic shuffle, with glittering e-piano and subdued rhythm guitar strokes, carving a mini-solo to install the sizzle. A feelgood tune is next , the highly personal "Una Valigia di Perche", (a suitcase of why) dealing with trials and tribulations of a travelling musician, not always an easy task when one has a family as well. "Enigma" is a track from the Trip catalog and its a more expansive adventure, a harsher climate where the keys and guitar settle into more progressive realm. The bass and drum configuration is on it like a car bonnet, an extended instrumental foundation painstakingly elaborated, shining some deserved light on Capasso considerable capabilities. The keyboard contributions are also most worthy of applause. The Ivan Graziani-penned "Monnalisa" is the proverbial epic here, clocking in at 8 and a half minutes, an arch-typical Italian language progressive rock canzone, with plenty of theatrical vocals, wrapped up in a semi boogie-woogie soundscape, an ideal moment with a live concert sequence. The grungy guitar is all brawn and muscle, almost a ZZ Top feel to the solo, the just oozes a wide variety of emotions, including oodles of perspiration. It also fulfills the ritual of introducing the band members with mini-spotlights, so as to show off their considerable talents. Its hot stuff! Keeping those traditions is crucial and a little Morricone reminder will never hurt, especially when its instantly recognizable as vintage cowboy pasta. When The Shadows classic "Apache" follows suite, images of dusty tumbleweeds and towering mesas take the journey not just to the other side of the Atlantic but also back in time. Now, I am not familiar with the I Quelli piece (the band that spawned PFM), yet "Una Bambolina che fa no no no" is a commemoration of the very early days of prog, especially in Italy, with unconcealed pop tendencies, muddied with some gritty guitar shavings, with a discernable the Kinks feel, in my opinion. The Lucio Battisti -composed "Il Tempo di Morire" (A Time to Die) keeps the good times rolling, another rock-blues exercise in restraint and homage to the influences. Carmine' fretboard chugging like a train on twisted tracks, smoky audience sing-along to boot and a sense of emotional synchronicity with concert-goers to shed the inhibitions and rock out. The saloon-like atmosphere is led by the rambling Sarno piano work , and the screeching lead guitar solo that had all the whiskey bottles rattling. In essence, this is what a true and blue live experience recording should transmit and this one shines ever so brightly. Remembering when music was fun. Five monster tracks to slay whatever hesitations one may have held in advance, blown to bits within the very first notes on "21st Century Schizoid Man", a mainstay of sonic brutalism in its infancy at the time (still the heaviest track ever composed, when taken into analytical context), and these seasoned musicians pull it off without any hint of weakness. "Lucky Man" is initially unrecognizable from the ELP original, a clever twist that comes to fruition only when Carmine starts singing the famous lyrics, and the magical chorus elicits smiles of recognition. The guitar-centric sections in such a live setting give this piece a much admirable kick in the back side, the delicate piano and rolling bass in full gear. The mythical Moog synthesizer solo is reproduced toa tee, as it would be a crime to even dare to alter such a bejewelled moment. The three PFM tracks are outright classics, the always impressive and elaborate "La Carrozza di Hans", a demanding labour of technical prowess, concentration and emotive expression, very obviously inspired by the previous KC track. The Sarno/Capasso tandem weave quite the web of sonic capture, the vocals intimately alluring, while the rhythm engine alternate expertly between cruise control and maximum acceleration. What really stirs the imagination is how the audience is fooled thrice into precocious applause. "Impressioni di Settembre" and "E'Festa" are monuments to eternity, the kind of musical rekindling that never caters to ennui, always a wonderful experience, after thousands of spins over half a century, much like "Firth of Fifth", incrusted with timeless melodies that continuously provide goosebumps for both the body and the mind. And that my friends, is what music is all about, and this recording is the second-best thing to having been in the audience. I was there. 4.5 dreamy stories

items.body: Review by alainPP — 1. "It Takes a Woman's Love (To Make a Man)" kicks things off with thunderous keyboards and vocals?dating back to the days when Robby and Steve traded licks; an explosive, short track that sets the tone for their signature rock style, blending heavy and folk elements.2. "Two Cents Worth" offers a similar vibe?short and energetic?though it lacks any real progressive flair.3. "Icarus - Borne on Wings of Steel" raises the bar?thank goodness, because anyone listening only to the first two tracks (as is common today) would miss out on this gem. A hard-rocking riff and vintage keyboards (featuring revolutionary Moog synths) combine to create a sort of proto-prog-metal sound. In 1975, there weren't many other bands doing this. The track relies on vocal harmonies, instrumental jamming, and?above all?a folk-prog-metal hybrid that was ahead of its time; the finale is ecstatic and defies description.4. "All the World" keeps the momentum going; it features backing vocals and orchestration, followed by a keyboard workout over a gritty riff?dynamic yet fierce. That riff reminds me of punk rock thanks to its latent aggression, while the sublime violin interlude adds a special touch unique to this band. The finale features staccato violin backing vocals reminiscent of Queen?back when both bands were experimenting with prog in their own distinct ways.5. "Child of Innocence" offers a breather after the side flip; it's a transitional track?starting with the energy of a potential radio edit (hard folk-rock) before shifting into a frenetic instrumental section that enters the realm of prog, with a hint of Thin Lizzy.6. "It's You" features violin and piano alongside a frantic folk rhythm?almost like a *bourr�e*?making it an electric and innovative track for its time. It feels like dancing in a Scottish pub on a stormy night while waiting to set sail again.7. "Mysteries and Mayhem" follows the "Child" formula: long enough to develop a prog atmosphere, yet short enough to keep the listener engaged. For me, this is the weakest track?whereas their long songs were always excellent, the shorter ones sometimes struggle to hold a prog fan's attention.8. "The Pinnacle" kicks off with a symphonic intro?grandiloquent, folk-infused prog metal at its peak! The tone, the vocals, the surrounding keyboards, and that majestic quality that made Kansas a spearhead of the genre. Personally, I'd classify them more as prog metal than symphonic rock?or perhaps right on the border between the two. The bridge?featuring a melody that Dream Theater would revisit much later?arrives while I'm talking; it just goes to show what a rock-solid track this is. Kerry and Steve show off their inventive keyboard skills; the symphonic element is front and center. A lingering, atmospheric feel, and plenty of emotion?though the guitar solo feels a bit too isolated for my taste, given the prominent role of Robby's violin. Then again, that's Kansas for you! (3.5)

items.body: Review by FrancescoProg — The birth of this new album was marked by difficult personal events and major changes within the band. In 2019, longtime co-founder Scott Kelly permanently left the group after serious domestic issues. This led Neurosis into a long period of pause and reflection. For this new phase, core members Steve Von Till, Jason Roeder, Dave Edwardson and Noah Landis enthusiastically welcomed Aaron Turner, a leading figure in post-metal, already frontman of Isis and Sumac, as the new guitarist and vocalist. Turner fit in perfectly, actively contributing to the songwriting with his creativity and talent. The album was recorded by producer Scott Evans in a fast process that resulted in an extremely raw sound.The album, speaks of spiritual and emotional survival in a difficult time, both globally and personally. The title itself sets, on one side, the image of a world on fire, a symbol of the environmental and geopolitical crises around us; on the other, the strength of love, which endures despite everything. This "burning world" also represents the hardships the band faced after Scott Kelly's departure, a time of great change and pain. The "undying love," instead, is the choice not to give up, to keep believing in empathy, love and the beauty of art, even when everything seems to fall apart. The album doesn't stick to pure violence, but also plays with tension and silence. Noah Landis has a key role, adding spectral synthesizers, industrial noises and samples that recall the darker Pink Floyd. Many tracks unfold through long, ritual crescendos, like the closing suite "Last Light" (17 minutes), which gradually turns into an industrial escalation.Aaron Turner, with his deep, cavernous and abstract growl, pairs perfectly with Steve Von Till's desperate screams. Alternating with these two voices are bassist Dave Edwardson's deep choruses and ghostly spoken word, creating a true tragic chorus that perfectly tells the story of the world's collapse."An Undying Love for a Burning World" is an album that grabs you right away, with its emotional charge and bold sonic choices. There are moments that struck me in particular.The album's opening is truly unforgettable for the intense emotional weight it conveys, a goosebump-inducing start. The instrumental introduction "We Are Torn Wide Open" builds an almost cinematic tension. The industrial drones and tribal tolls give a sense of emptiness and looming danger.In "Mirror Deep," halfway through the track, the music slows down, almost stops, creating a suspended atmosphere, then explodes into a section of incredible heaviness. It's right at this moment that Aaron Turner screams the line "True wealth between our fingers slip, as we count the dead". A passage that fuses the melancholic force of post-metal with a shattering impact. Noah Landis's synths take the track to near-spatial levels.Then there's "Blind": the central instrumental section opens into stretched, hypnotic dynamics, recalling the more psychedelic Pink Floyd and krautrock, slowing the pace and leaving room for the music. The following contrast, between clean vocals and powerful growls over an imposing wall of guitars, is one of the album's most intense and surprising passages."Seething and Scattered" has direct, syncopated riffs full of tension, spilling into an unexpected rhythmic turn. Jason Roeder's drumming creates an almost tribal atmosphere before the track heads into spectacular progressions.Finally, the ending of "Last Light" (a 17-minute suite), a colossal suite that closes with the desperate, anguished cry "What have we done?", which fades into a loop of industrial noise, drones and feedback.This album is undoubtedly a masterpiece. Turner didn't just replace Scott Kelly; he became a true creative engine, bringing his deep growl and his unique approach. It's not a nostalgia move, but a work that shows how Neurosis are still the kings of post-metal, able to reinvent themselves and rise even from major personal hardships.

items.body: Review by FrancescoProg — "Let's THRAK Again" is a tribute to the 1995 album THRAK by King Crimson, with the approval and blessing of founder Robert Fripp. This album is Stick Men's first studio record in over ten years, a project that brings together two longtime members of King Crimson's rhythm section from that era, bassist Tony Levin and drummer Pat Mastelotto, along with Touch Guitar virtuoso Markus Reuter.The trio wanted to recreate the same controlled chaos and the energy of the original album, describing it as "instrumental chamber music". They composed and arranged the twelve tracks to be performed live as a lean trio, with minimal use of sampling or electronics.To offer a truly unique experience, the band decided not to release just one mix, but two completely different versions of the same recorded material. The first, Reel One, mixed by Stefano Castagna, follows a track sequence devised by Tony Levin, focusing on a very specific sonic vision and philosophy. The second, Reel Two (yet to be released), mixed by Fabio Trentini, will feature a different sequence, curated by Mastelotto and Reuter, and uses (they say) entirely new sound choices and audio approaches. All tracks are previously unreleased compositions, recorded specifically for this project. The trio described the whole work as a series of pieces created from scratch to develop an "original sonic vocabulary".Stick Men themselves described the album's musical style as "heavy prog with nothing short of explosive kinetic energy", and I agree with that definition. A sound that blends the typical elements of darker, more mathematical progressive rock with industrial, art rock and avant-garde metal influences. The songs have intricate structures and odd time signatures, driven by powerful, massive riffs. Even though they're only three, the simultaneous combination of melodic lines and a rocky bass creates a dense, intense orchestral sound.The album alternates moments of pure instrumental acceleration with softer, more rarefied ambient passages, keeping a tense and always experimental atmosphere. The rhythm section blends the power of acoustic sounds with industrial samples, loops and electronic pads.My favorite tracks are: "Swimming in Tea", which is without a doubt the track that surprised me the most, chosen as the lead single, with an immediate structure and the special feature of having Markus Reuter on vocals, before giving way to a memorable Tony Levin Chapman Stick solo.The opening track, "Let's THRAK Again", for its ability to reproduce the complex rhythms and the "heavy prog" impact that distinguished the original 1995 King Crimson album."Haggin Triptych", an instrumental suite divided into three parts (Renoir, Carriage Parade and Yosemite Sunset), which is a masterful example of rhythmic interlocking. A triumphant and thrilling return, a true masterpiece of composition and musical performance, a must-buy for both King Crimson devotees and lovers of heavier avant-prog. Essential album.

They played excerpts/two-person versions of three of the songs from the new record which was totally composed on Sibelius using classical composers like Stravinsky, Reich, Bjork, Berg, Ravel, Autechre, Debussy, and many others as influences to their Fusion. And there are vocals--and full orchestras! But at the core/base of it all are still the maximalist fusion of the amazing virtuosi JD and DOMi. For any aged music lover I think DOMi and JD are offering something new, innovative, technically superior (like the "good ole days), and progressive. For any disbelievers of the talent emanating from this duo (and this album) I urge you to view the "DOMi & JD Beck - Metropole Orkest" video footage on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uz5ysfMtbcQMuch of the material that ended up on the Who Asked? album is there being performed live with full orchestra.FULL REVIEW COMING as I get further into the music. items.body: Nolwenn Boyet and Ronni Gauderat make up the French duo Buzzkill. Active since 2024, Buzzkill previously released an EP on Ganache Records. For their debut album, “Wasteland”, they joined forces with Manic Depression Records, a move that will help expand their audience. “Wasteland” blends Cold-Wave and Minimal-Electro influences, with a raw, uncompromising sound driven by icy synth textures and deep, brooding basslines. Nolwenn Boyet’s cold, detached vocal delivery complements the music throughout. I spoke with both Buzzkill musicians about the making of “Wasteland”. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Buzzkill interview Q: Let’s start with the origins of Buzzkill. When and how did the band come together, and what are your individual musical backgrounds? How did those experiences inspire you to form Buzzkill? Nolwenn: We created a band shortly after meeting Ronni. At first, the project was very different from what it is today. We didn’t have the ambition to make something professional out of it, we just wanted to make music and spend time together. At the time we were a trio, with Ronni on bass and vocals, Axelle on synths and me on drums. When Axelle left the band, we wanted to try something else. We started experimenting with a duo setup where I took over the vocals and synths, and the drums became electronic. We quickly felt that something was working. We compose together quite naturally and found a good balance as a duo. At the end of 2024, we wrote our first EP, which was a starting point for us. It really captured the beginning of Buzzkill and helped define our identity. Ronni: I started playing music at 15, as a drummer in a Grunge band, which later became a Rock’n’roll band that I still play in today. At the same time, I taught myself guitar and started several other projects, including a Shoegaze band and a swamp Garage band with which I toured for eight years and released two albums. Today, I’m also working on a Synth-Punk duo alongside my other projects. My musical background is quite eclectic, maybe even a bit chaotic, but I’ve always liked moving from one style to another. The creative process is what motivates me the most. I just like writing music and exploring different directions. Nolwenn: My journey as a musician actually started with Buzzkill. I had never sung, played synths or composed music before. I had only played a bit of drums when I was a teenager. Meeting Ronni is what pushed me to get into music. I like this kind of unexpected path and I’m still learning as I go. Ronni and I come from very different musical backgrounds, but we share the same approach. Keeping things simple and raw. Q: Earlier this year, you released the debut album of Buzzkill, “Wasteland”. Looking back on the entire creative process, what stands out to you most? What was your vision for the album in terms of its sound and production? Ronni: What probably stood out the most to us were the conditions in which we recorded the album. We did it in a garden shed, during a heatwave. It was a strange feeling to create such cold music while being in 40 degree heat. Maybe that’s what naturally led us towards the atmosphere of “Wasteland”. Nolwenn: Like for our EP, we recorded everything ourselves. We used pretty much the same equipment, but we had improved a lot in the way we used it and knew more clearly where we wanted to go. With “Wasteland”, we wanted to create something that felt more like a complete album, with a stronger overall atmosphere. We also wanted to lean further into the Electronic side of the project. We spent more time working on synth textures, drum sounds and the atmosphere of each track. I also discovered my voice more and found the way I wanted to use it. For the bass, we wanted to keep that raw and upfront feeling, with a sound that doesn’t feel overproduced. It was already part of the EP’s identity, and I think it defines a big part of what Buzzkill sounds like. We were also careful about which songs we wanted to include. That’s why the album only has seven tracks. It felt complete that way, and we liked the idea of keeping it short and intense. For the mastering, we worked again with Mathis Kolkoz (Blind Delon), who also mastered the EP. We really like his work and trusted him for this. Q: “Wasteland” is a bleak and evocative title. What does it represent to you, and which emotions shaped the music and inspired the lyrics? Nolwenn: “Wasteland” represents our vision of an apocalyptic future. It’s a deliberately exaggerated and pessimistic vision, but deep down it doesn’t feel that unrealistic today. We wanted a strong title that would immediately evoke an empty and hopeless landscape. We were quite inspired by the post-apocalyptic and desert aesthetics of movies like “Dune” and “Mad Max”, as well as games like “Fallout” and “Borderland”. The lyrics came from our anger and anxiety about the current ecological and social crises, but also from the feeling of injustice around the fact that the most vulnerable people are always the first to suffer the consequences. Through “Wasteland”, we imagine a future where no one can escape the collapse, not even the most privileged. It’s a sad thought that maybe the only moment when these inequalities could disappear is when we’re all facing the end of the world. Q: In a way, “Wasteland” feels like the soundtrack to a world in decline – a place where people are struggling with both themselves and the reality surrounding them. How personal is this album, and what is your perspective, both as artists and as individuals, on the state of the world today? Nolwenn: This album is very personal because it comes from the way we experience the world today and the anxiety it creates in us. But I think it speaks to a lot of people, especially younger generations who know they’ll grow old in this world, or at least in what will be left of it. As I’m answering this interview we’ve reached 42°C in our city. There are major forest fires happening in our country and people are dying because of the heat, while political responses still seem completely disconnected from the reality we’re facing. It’s become impossible not to think every day about what the world will be like in 10, 20 or 30 years, and under what conditions we’ll be living. “Wasteland” is our cathartic way of putting words and sounds to the distress we’re feeling lately. Q: I’ve always found it fascinating that some of the darkest, most nihilistic themes can inspire such compelling and even danceable music. There seems to be an intriguing contradiction between despair and movement. How important is that contrast to Buzzkill, and what role does music play for you as a means of expression? Ronni: This contradiction is very much part of the DNA of Post-Punk. We’ve always liked that contrast in bands like Joy Division. We like the idea that music can make you want to dance while talking about very dark subjects. We also felt that fast tempos and repetitive rhythms were the best way to express tension and urgency. If we have to live in a world that’s falling apart, we might as well dance through it. Q: Let’s talk about the live Buzzkill experience. What can audiences expect from a Buzzkill performance, and what atmosphere or emotions do you hope to create on stage? How do your songs evolve in a live setting compared to their studio versions? Ronni: Live we try to keep things intense and direct. We don’t talk much, sometimes not at all. We like to step back and let the music take the lead. We try to build a set where the atmosphere can evolve naturally. We like playing almost without breaks because we enjoy the feeling of a 45 min set that keeps moving, with very little time to come back down. It’s a way to convey that overwhelming feeling we have. The bass also brings something very organic and physical to the live experience. I play it through both a bass amp and a guitar amp. Q: Finally, what are your expectations and ambitions for Buzzkill following the release of “Wasteland”? What can listeners look forward to in the near future? Nolwenn: We didn’t really expect “Wasteland” to get much attention at the beginning. We just told ourselves: let’s do our thing and see what happens. We were lucky to meet our friend and manager Stephy just before its release, and she really helped us give the album more visibility. Our main goal now is to keep defending the album on stage, in France of course, but also to start playing in other European countries. We’d like to keep developing the project, see where this album can take us, and keep writing because it’s what drives us in life. We also want to keep surrounding ourselves with people we appreciate, discover new projects from the underground scene, and share the stage with artists we love. We’re already thinking about the next album and we’ve started writing again. We want to explore new directions, maybe something a bit more Electro-Punk, with more repetitive and hypnotic structures, while still keeping what defines Buzzkill. To finish, we just want to say to everyone reading this: keep supporting the underground scene and independent artists. Keep going to concerts in dark and humid caves, discovering local bands and getting lost on Bandcamp. This counterculture only survives because people choose to support it. Thanks for that. And thank you, Stéphane and Side-line for the interview 🙂 Nolwenn and Ronni – Buzzkill

items.body: Krieg-B will release a new album, “Concrete Dominion,” on October 24, 2026, the same date as the band’s performance at the 19th Elektrisch Festival at Club Seilerstraße in Zwickau, Germany. The album comes via Emmo.biz Records. The label describes “Concrete Dominion” as combining the raw energy of EBM, darkwave and industrial music with powerful rhythms, massive basslines and hypnotic sequences. The album is built on the tension between human impulse and the cold architecture of machines, aiming for a soundtrack of urban atmosphere, mechanical force and relentless movement, a dark and intense journey through concrete landscapes where rhythm becomes the driving force. Formats and festival tie-in “Concrete Dominion” will be available as a CD with twelve tracks and an LP with eight tracks across two sides. The CD track list runs “Bite,” “Machinehead,” “Kill The Light,” “Cold Fragments” (feat. Misty), “Perestroika,” “Locked,” “Blackout,” “Libera Nos A Malo,” “Par Dessus Les Cendres,” “Molotov,” “New Zone Of Terror” and “Signal Ahead.” The LP carries eight of those tracks: side one holds “Bite,” “Machinehead,” “Kill The Light” and “Cold Fragments” (feat. Misty), while side two holds “Locked,” “Libera Nos A Malo,” “Molotov” and “Signal Ahead.” Emmo.biz Records is also selling bundled sets tied to the Zwickau show. A “Supporter” set pairs the LP and CD with a 10″ festival sampler featuring an exclusive 12″ mix of “Kill The Light” plus a ticket to the 19th Elektrisch Festival, and a “Fan” set bundles the LP, CD and the 10″ sampler without the ticket. A standard “Combo” set with just the LP and CD is limited to 77 copies, with the vinyl pressed on red and black streaked wax. About Krieg-B Krieg-B is a French-Belgian duo formed in June 2023 by Dominique Lallement, also known for his work as Kriegbereit, Cobalt 60 and K Bereit, and Benoît Buyse, who records as Dreadfool, Anamorphosis and Nihiliste. Based in Reims, France, the pair build on decades of industrial, EBM and darkwave music. Krieg-B released its debut album, “War Drums’ Resonance,” in September 2024 through Emmo.biz Records, in a limited edition of 77 copies that paired the 11-track record with a bonus disc holding a cover of Cabaret Voltaire’s “Nag Nag Nag” and a T-shirt. The band was confirmed for the 19th Elektrisch Festival line-up in April 2026, alongside Portion Control, Escalator, Oszylator and Cyborg Projekt X. “Concrete Dominion” is the duo’s second full-length album.

items.body: Melbourne-based gothic/darkwave/industrial duo Velatine has released the Dead Radio EP on July 28, 2026, available digitally via Bandcamp and streaming platforms including Spotify. The four-track EP centers on new versions of “Playing with the Orbits”, a song the band first released as a single earlier in 2026. Playing with the Orbits – Dead Radio EP by Velatine Tracklist for Velatine’s ‘Dead Radio EP’ The tracklist comprises “Dead Radio Remix”, “Late Night Club Mix”, “Dead Radio Remix (Extended)” and “Absinthe Remix”. The closing “Absinthe Remix” combines acoustic guitar, violin and industrial electronic elements with the duo’s established gothic and darkwave sound. “Playing with the Orbits” was written by Velatine member Loki Lockwood about the 2019 murder of Bianca Devins, an American teenager killed by a man she had met online, and the subsequent circulation of images from the crime scene on social media. The song had previously been released with a different vocalist; the “Dead Radio Remix” on this EP is presented as a reworked version that better reflects the project’s current direction, shaped by the band’s recent live performances. About Velatine Velatine is a gothic/darkwave duo from Melbourne, Australia, formed by Loki Lockwood and Maggie Alley in late 2021. Lockwood had previously been active as a producer in the projects The Drones and Spencer P. Jones before starting Velatine. The duo released its first seven-inch single, “Comic” / “No God”, in March 2022, followed by the industrial-leaning track “Deadly Requiem” that August and a second seven-inch, “Whisper Park” / “One and Only”, in November 2022, accompanied by a video directed by Mathew T Ellery. A remix of “No God”, paired with footage from the 1973 film “Frankenstein”, followed shortly after. In February 2023, Velatine released its debut album, “I Won’t Be Civilised”, on Spooky Records, preceded by the singles “No God”, “Comic” and “Whisper Park”. The band has continued to perform live regularly since, a period the duo credits with shaping the more industrial-leaning direction heard on the “Dead Radio EP”.
